We respectfully recommend:
(1) That, because of the introduction into the evidence, necessarily and unavoidably of secret technical data, the publication of which, according to the witnesses most concerned, would not be in the public interest at this time, none of the evidence or exhibits relating to any top secret, secret, restricted or confidential matters be published except with the approval of the government in consultation with the heads of the services, departments or organizations concerned.

Mr. Speaker, in

While it is sitting, and until its existence terminates, it is not subordinate to any body.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO LOAN PROVISIONS-CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION

speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved the second reading of bill No. 306, to amend the National Housing Act, 1944.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this bill, I would like to comment upon the amendments to the National Housing Act which we seek at this time. The bill itself is rather voluminous. However, the real changes are fewer than would appear.
Hon. members will recall that at the last session of parliament the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act was passed. The act provides under section 18:
The Corporation shall, on behalf of His Majesty and in the place of the minister, have, exercise and perform all rights, powers, duties, liabilities and functions of the minister under the housing acts or under any contract entered into under the said acts, except the authority of the minister under the said acts to pay moneys out of the consolidated revenue fund, or under section twelve of the National Housing Act, 1944, to make grants for slum clearance.
This bill contains thirty-eight clauses, of which twenty-six clauses make no substantial change to the National Housing Act other than to give effect to this transfer of authority which I have just described. I do not think hon. members will wish me to review each one of these twenty-six clauses, particularly as they do not involve any change in principle or policy. I will, therefore, limit my remarks to

Housing Act
an explanation of the other twelve clauses of the bill, which in varying degree, affect the operations of the act.
I will deal first with clause 2 which deletes, from the definition of the cost of construction, the proviso that in the case of a loan for the construction of a house on a farm, the appraised value of the land shall be deemed to be not more than 20 per cent of the actual expenditure and other expenses and charges. This deletion is desirable to make the definition of cost of construction conform to a subsequent amendment changing the basis for loans for farm housing.
Clause 3 of the bill redefines economic rental of a family housing unit. No change in principle is involved, and the purpose of the amendment is to clarify the intent of the definition.
Similarly clause 4 clarifies the meaning of the definition of housing project. We wish to make it clear that in the case of a rental housing project, buildings other than houses necessary to a planned development may be included in the lending value.
Clause 5 of the bill introduces an amendment to the definition of a metropolitan area. "Metropolitan area" is now defined as a city together with one or more adjacent municipalities in the same province. We wish to delete the phrase "in the same province" which serves no useful purpose. The adjacency of Ottawa and Hull is the main reason for this change. This clause also redefines the "minister" as the "Minister of Reconstruction and Supply" instead of the "Minister of Finance". When speaking on the resolution I outlined the administrative changes which had taken place.
The change contemplated by clause 7, besides replacing "minister" by "corporation" is rearrangement of order and involves no change in principle. This clause was previously contained in the section dealing particularly with farm housing, whereas the travelling expenses allowed to lending institutions are equally applicable to other joint loans. We feel that it would be more logical and would avoid confusion if this section formed a part of section 3 of the Act.
Clause 8 provides for the heading of part I, "Housing for home owners" to follow rather than to precede section 3, because section 3 has application not only to loans for home owners, but also to housing for rental purposes and farm housing.
Clause 9 widens the scope of the operations of the National Housing Act in that the corporation will be given authority to make loans on houses where the owner has a leasehold interest in the land. At present it is not
possible to make a National Housing Act loan in our national park areas. The Department of Mines and Resources quite properly is unwilling to sell land to a prospective home owner in our national parks. However, they are willing to grant a lease for a satisfactory term. I think hon. members will agree that it is desirable for the terms of the National Housing Act to be available in such areas as Banff and Jasper. It is not the intention to use this authority, if granted, to promote National Housing Act loans on leasehold land in urban areas. In most cases the crown in right of Canada or in right of the provinces will be the owner of the land. Consideration has been given to qualifying for National Housing Act loans only leasehold land owned by the dominion or the provinces. It may well prove to be the case that it will be desirable to finance housing on leasehold land owned by individuals who are willing to arrange leases of sufficient term and under conditions which adequately safeguard the interests of His Majesty as mortgagee.
Clause 10 defines the type of security to be taken with leasehold property. It is complementary to Clause 9.
Clause 10 also provides for loans to home owners for a period of twenty-five years instead of twenty years as at present. It also provides that in areas adequately planned the loan may be made for a term of thirty years. When speaking to the resolution I dealt rather fully with the reasons for this change. I would like to repeat that the increased costs of construction have resulted in larger loans. The veteran is faced with heavier monthly repayments on the larger loan. We feel that under the present system of lending, there is no great risk incurred by increasing the term of amortization to twenty-five years. Monthly payments of principal, interest and one-twefth of the annual taxes afford a large measure of protection. It is interesting to note that under the National Housing Act in the United States, the most usual term of loan is twenty-five years. It is to be remembered that the period of risk is not the period of amortization. For instance, in the case of a twenty year loan, 50 per cent has been repaid in twelve years. In the case of a twenty-five year loan, 50 per cent of the loan has been repaid in sixteen years. Generally I believe that when about onedialf of the original loan has been repaid, the mortgage is well out of the risk area, not only because of reduced amount owing, but also because of the long record of payment by the borrower. We intend to apply the extra five years of amortization particularly to types of housing which we wish to encourage. For example, we feel that the extremely small four
Housing Act

room bungalows of some seven hundred square feet are not the type of construction which should be encouraged by a loan with longer amortization. We would prefer for the same home owner to arrange a larger mortgage with the longer amortization on a one and a half storey six room house even if the upper two rooms are not finshed until a later date. Extra financing of 13-9 per cent can be made available with longer amortization without increasing the monthly payments of principal and interest. It would be our intention to apply the twenty-five year amortization basis only to the mere desirable classes of property which we wish to encourage.
Clause 13 introduces a new section-section 4A-to give authority to the corporation to enter into agreements to safeguard the interests of His Majesty in loans on leasehold land.
Hon. members will recall that in the War Measures Act provision was made by order in council for housing under the integrated plan. In my remarks upon the resolution I reviewed operations under this plan and indicated its terms and conditions. We feel that the integrated plan, which this year will produce some two or three thousand units, lends promise of even greater development next year. We feel that the plan is admirably suited for the best interests of the owner, builder and the government. It is affording control upon the sale price of new houses; it is assuring that materials are channeled into veterans' housing. Clause 13 also gives authority to the corporation to continue with this plan after the order in council is repealed. It will also be noted that provision is made for the appropriations already voted for loans and losses under part I to be used to finance loans under the integrated plan.
Under clause 14 a change is made to section 6 (1) of the National Housing Act. Hon. members will notice this subsection gives authority to determine the amount of the loss in respect of a loan under part I. It is quite evident that the intention of this subsection was to give authority for determining losses under all parts of the act. The amendment which I propose gives effect to this intention.
This clause also introduces two new subsections, 6(3) and 6(4). Subsection 3 is necessary to carry out the powers given in respect of the integrated housing plan when it becomes necessary to purchase a house which, under the integrated agreement, the builder may require the corporation to buy. Subsection 4 provides for the funds to make these purchases out of the appropriation provided by section 7 of part I.

It will be noted that clause 14 rearranges the manner in which regulations are made for the administrative functions of parts I and III of the act. No very great change in principle is involved, but now that the corporation is taking over the main administrative duties in operating the act, it is felt that the revision proposed will be more practical. The governor in council will continue to make regulations on these administrative matters where necessary, but it will be noticed that the new section 5(2) of the act provides that the corporation may prescribe procedural matters in connection with an application for a loan, the calculation of the cost of construction, standards, and whether it is desirable to take additional security.
Clause 15 substitutes the corporation for the minister, but makes no change in the length of amortization for rental housing comparable to the lengthening of the amortization period we seek for home owners. Section 8(2) of the National Housing Act provides for a term of loan for rental housing not in excess of twenty years. Where the project is protected by community planning and appropriate zoning, the loan may be for a period not in excess of twenty-five years. Although we would like to see an increased amount of rental housing, we do not believe that lengthening the amortization period will have that effect. We believe that it is not advisable to make any change in this section at this time.
Clause 15 introduces additional lending facilities under new section 9A of the National Housing Act which I reviewed when speaking to the resolution. We are in very short supply of housing in outlying areas. This is particularly true in mining and lumbering communities. From all points of view it would be desirable for on-site operations of lumbering and mining companies to employ a larger number of men, and particularly married men. The day of the bunk house is over, even for single men. Mining and lumbering companies are having difficulties in inducing married men to enter their employ because of the impossibility of bringing their families with them. We feel that every encouragement should be given to the development of family housing units in outlying areas, particularly adjacent to on-site operations of the lumbering and mining companies. The type of housing will vary according to location. It will range all the way from temporary housing units on skids to fully modern permanent houses. The development of such programme is hampered bj^ the lack of materials. It is also restricted by lack of financing facilities. Loans on this type of security are almost a blind spot in our credit

Housing Act
structure. In many cases they are so remote or are located in such unmortgagable property that the mortgage lending institutions cannot provide financing. The capital investment for a substantial number of units places too great a strain upon the working capital position of the lumbering or mining company. Bank loans, besides being a demand obligation and current liability of the lumbering and mining company, are generally made with terms of repayment which provide too short a period to be appropriate for housing units, particularly when the company is depending upon the rentals from such housing units to provide the cash to liquidate the loan. The proposed amendment outlines in detail the type of loan which we propose. The main features are:
1.	The loans are made to, or are guaranteed by, the lumbering or mining company.
2.	The term of amortization may be as long as fifteen years.
3.	The rate of interest is 4 per cent.
4.	The company cannot earn on its investment in the housing project more thian the 4 per cent interest rate. Any current surplus must be used for a rent reduction fund. Should an equity exist after the loan is repaid, and the company has recovered its investment with not more than the 4 per cent interest, the value of the residue shall be used for charitable purposes or community benefits.
5.	Minimum standards for this type of housing will be very flexible because the type of housing, the locality', and the needs will vary greatly.
6.	The maximum loan will be 80 per cent of the lending value, although in many cases I think that the loans will be considerably less than 80 per cent.
7.	Provision is made for the sale of such houses by the company to home owners. In such cases the company will remain on the covenant of the mortgage even for that portion which has been sold to a home owner. Provision will be made that if the home owner's account is current, default in the blanket mortgage will not prejudice his position.
S.	The corporation, before recommending a loan for approval by the governor in council, will satisfy itself through inquiry to other government departments that the area in which the housing is to be erected has a productive period sufficient to justify the loan, and that the proposed housing is necessary in the area, and generally will result in additional employment.
I feel that this proposal will be a very valuable addition to the lending facilities under the National Housing Act. Many lumbering 63260-251
and mining companies are interested in housing and willing to do something about it. In most cases that have been brought to our attention, the obstacle has been a lack of suitable financing even more than the lack of materials. I would hope that it might be possible for prefabricated housing to be used for this purpose, particularly in areas where on-site skilled building labour is very scarce. In my opinion, the proposed amendment is the most efficient, cheapest and expeditious manner of meeting a very real need.
Clause 15 puts in statutory form the home conversion plan as new section 9B. There is only a modest amount in the estimates for additional development of the home conversion plan because it is not likely that many projects will be undertaken during this fiscal year. Materials are in short supply, costs are high, the number of houses suitable for conversion under the plan are few, and even those houses which are suitable cannot, in most cases, be vacated to allow the conversion to take place. As I mentioned in my remarks on the resolution, there are two hundred and sixty properties which have been converted, creating some twenty-one hundred units. It is our intention to repeal the orders in council under which this plan was authorized. We seek this new section of the National Housing Act because the corporation must continue to hold, operate and manage existing properties. Moreover, we would like to be in a position to convert any buildings suitable for the purpose, few in number though they may be.
Clause 15 also reenacts section 10 of the act, which gives the governor in council power to make regulations for rental housing. The changes proposed for new section 10 of the National Housing Act are similar to those that I described earlier for new section 5 of the National Housing Act which provides for the same type of regulation for housing for home owners.
Clause 17 of the bill proposes a modification to the authority already granted to the insurance companies to make direct investments in low or moderate rental property. It will be remembered that such investments when approved by the corporation, are subject to a guarantee by the government ensuring a 2£ per cent return to the insurance company. The insurance companies may invest up to 5 per cent of their Canadian assets under section 11.
Some of the insurance companies are showing great interest in this form of investment and would like to develop in Canada projects similar to those of the Metropolitan Life in the United States such as the Parkchester multiple unit development in New York and the
Housing Act

horizontal developments in other communities. In light of our very great need for housing of this type, I am sure that the house will commend our efforts to stimulate the interest of the insurance companies -in this field of endeavour.
We believe that section 11 is satisfactory in its present form, except for one factor. The first step towards the development of projects either individually or on a national basis is the acquisition of land suitable for the purpose. Experience both in Canada and the United States has shown that this must be done some time before the project can be determined in final form. In order to secure land at a reasonable price, some degree of secrecy must be maintained. In some cases this can be achieved by securing options, in other cases, the land must be purchased. It would be most inadvisable to secure firm bids for construction from a number of contractors while the acquisition of the site was still under negotiation. Some companies are anxious to plan on a national basis, and for various reasons do not wish to proceed with all projects simultaneously. Opportunities to secure very desirable sites arise from time to time and it would be desirable for the companies to be in a position to acquire land which would be developed over the next two or three years.
The legislation in its present form makes such investment legal for life companies-* including the purchase of the land or an option -only when the corporation has approved the project in all detail including the cost of land, the cost of construction, design, lay-out, rental levels, etc. The existing section contemplates simultaneous acquisition of land and approval of the project including the cost of construction. This is not only impracticable but also increases the cost of the project and makes an orderly two or three year programme virtually impossible. Even if the land is acquired and the project approved in the same year, and listing the land as an asset in the annual statement of the company is not involved. No authority exists. There is provision in the insurance laws of the state of New York to allow an orderly approach to the problem.
Therefore, with the concurrence of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, I propose this amendment making it possible with suitable safeguards such as prior approval by the corporation, for life companies to acquire or option land suitable for such purpose. The corporation will, at the time approval is given, ensure that:

(a)	The land is suitable and that the corporation will be willing to approve the project on the land at a later date.
(b)	Only land within the over-all plans of the life company for projects will be approved for purchase.
(c>
The amount of land so purchased will not be greater than can be developed within the limitation of 5 per cent of Canadian assets of the company. Roughly, the maximum purchases allowed will be one half of one per cent of the company's Canadian assets.
(d)	The project will proceed within a reasonable period of time and there are no speculative influences in the purchase.
Inside land and even serviced land in residential fringe areas is not plentiful. We must ensure that too much of such land is not acquired for development by life companies in the distant future to the detriment and disadvantage of others who wish to erect residential property on the land in the near future.
Under this section, the guarantee to the life companies only becomes effective after the project has been approved by the corporation and construction commences. Land held for a future project is not revenue producing and it would be inappropriate for any guarantee of interest return to be applicable. We propose, that when determining the cost of construction at the time the project is approved, to include the cost of land previously acquired and to allow, as an addition to such cost, the taxes paid less any net revenue from the use of the land. We will not consider as part of the cost of construction interest on the cost of the land from the date of acquisition to the time the project is started.
Clause 19 repeals section 14 of the act and substitutes a new section providing for financing new farm housing. The existing provisions have not worked well. Except where a lending institution, willing to make the loan on the new house, is the existing mortgagee, no provision is made for refinancing an existing encumbrance. Even under such circumstances and in all other cases, the section contemplates farm land as one part, and the farm home another part of the farm. Financing has been difficult under such provisions and no loans have been made.
The amendment now proposed authorizes loans up to $5,000, the cost of the farm house or two-thirds of the appraised value of the farm, whichever is the least. If the farm is mortgaged, refinancing can take place so that the loan may be $8,000, the cost of the house and amount to repay the existing mortgage, or two-thirds of the appraised value of the

Housing Act
farm whichever is the least. The interest is 44 per cent and the term of the loan twenty years.
The method of appraisal has been revised and is comparable to the method used in regular farm lending. It will be noted that where sufficient equity in the farm land exists, the equity in the new farm home can be financed by that means.
Revision of minimum standards and specifications will take place. Suitable flexible requirements will be devised to ensure that sound standards of construction will be reconciled with varying local conditions and requirements.
We will try to convince the lending institutions to enter into an agreement with the corporation to make loans under this section. We wish to avoid blind spots in coverage such as we have had in the past. Although the mortgage companies are not wildly enthusiastic about farm loans at the moment, I believe they, like ourselves, are anxious to see that the facilities of the act are available to all Canadians. Their cooperation under the recent arrangement to make non-farm National Housing Act loans in the smaller outlying communities is evidence of this desire.
Hon. members will immediately recognize that this change puts the corporation into the farm loan business. This is deliberate because a farm home is an inseparable part of the farm. If we mean business in promoting and financing new farm housing the loans cannot follow an urban pattern. We prefer the principle of joint "loans with a lending institution in the pattern of the National Housing Act rather than direct loans in the manner of the Canadian farm loan board. I therefore propose the amendment on that basis and expect that it will be effective. Should I be wrong, other techniques will be found because, although we like the proposed joint loan approach, the important end result is success in making these facilities available to farmers throughout the country.
I propose that this section come into force upon proclamation. Agreements with lending institutions must be worked out. Forms of joint mortgages for each province must be determined and in this respect we intend to break some new ground especially in the case of grain-growing farms. The old form of mortgage, together with a crop share lease, was not good enough even twenty years ago. We have no intention of imposing default on all housing act borrowers within an area just because there happens to be a general crop failure in that area. We will want full rights of col-63260- 251i
lection from borrowers able to pay and will insist upon an adequate escape clause to postpone amounts owing by the borrower when, due to conditions beyond his control, he is unable to pay. Towards this end we will be consulting with the provinces so that their legislation, protective and otherwise, will fit National Housing Act farm mortgage deeds. This will take time and. it is not likely that this section can be proclaimed for two or three months.
There are in this house a number of hon. members very familiar with the need for farm housing and who have had experience in the farm mortgage field. When we come to discuss the bill, section by section, I will welcome their comments. I think that this section is based on sound principles and will prove effective. Nevertheless, I am ready to accept suggestions for its improvement. It is an important section in light of the need of new and improved housing in the farm field, in the years to come.
This, Mr. Speaker, has been a rather lengthy review of the major changes which we propose in the National Housing Act. I have attempted to touch upon each change of major import and principle. As we go through the bill clause by clause, hon. members will have the opportunity of asking questions about changes which I have not specifically mentioned today.
There is one change which might have been included in my remarks. The act in its present form gives authority for loans for a maximum number of years. Take for example, a loan under part I for twenty years with the first of the progress payments being made on January 1,	1946. Mortgage practice and
convenience results in mortgage deed being drawn in a form that the borrower makes the first of his two hundred and forty monthly payments on, say, May 1, being a month or two after the completion of the house. Technically it might be argued that authority under the act only allows a loan to run until January 1, 1S66. Changes are included in the present amendments to allow the period of the loan to run from the date of the completion of the house rather than from the date of the first advance.
I would like to call hon. members' attention to the fact that although "corporation" has been substituted for "minister" throughout the act, no change has been made in the sections dealing with appropriations. We propose to rely on relevant clauses in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act which authorize the minister to advance moneys from the appropriations to the corporation for the purposes of the act.
Housing Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO LOAN PROVISIONS-CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill and the important statement which the minister made on the resolution stage are a new departure in the handling of the housing shortage in this country. They indicate to me something which I am sure everyone in the house and in the country will be very glad to hear-that the government has at last come to grips with the number one problem in the country, the housing of our people, and particularly of the returned men who obviously are bearing the brunt of the housing shortage. But at the same time, and while we welcome this evidence that the government has come to grips with the problem, surely that statement and this bill emphasize the previous lack of government policy in connection with this great problem. Surely the measures proposed by the minister and the things he has done in the last few months are proof of the government's failure to face a situation which has now prevailed in acute form for a year. And surely it shows that their attitude has been a passive waiting for improvement rather than an active attempt to deal with the matter.
The chief criticism that one can make of the statement and of the bill is that very simple one, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is a telling one too-that the bill is exactly a year late. This bill, and the appointment of the expediter of building materials and the concentration of housing activities under one minister, should have been brought into force at the last session of the last parliament, just before the end of the war, when victory was in sight. The need was apparent then, and plans should have been laid then. Had that been done, we would not have had the minister's statement the other day that the worst is yet to come, and his estimate that in the spring of 1947 the situation will be twenty per cent worse than it is now. I suggest that the "grin and bear it" stuff that the minister has given to the house would have been acceptable last year. The Canadian people would have realized the difficulties and, with such proposals as the minister is making now, and knowing that something was being done about it, they would have been willing last year to face a worsening of the situation in the spring of 1946 and to "grin and bear it." But this year the Canadian people will not find such a statement in any way acceptable. They will, I believe, look upon it as a confession of failure on the part of the government.
Having made that criticism, I want to refer to some of the good parts of this proposal, not only the bill but the executive measures which the minister has taken. There are,
IMr. Howe.]
apart from some very proper developments, and, I might say, modernization of the procedure under the National Housing Act, five most important new departures which the minister has taken.
First of all, housing has been centralized under one minister, where it should always have been.
Second, we have a full-time executive charged apparently with the development of over-all policy; and it is my understanding that that wholetime executive is a very able man indeed.
Third, we have what we obviously needed for many months-for a whole year-and that is an expediter of building materials. This, I understand, is to be one of the functions of the coordinator of housing. In addition we have the committee that the minister has mentioned, set up to deal with the building material problem. He tells us that progress has been made, and we are very glad indeed to hear it.
Fourth, and very important, the National Housing Act has been redesigned to meet Canada's particular needs. I think it is right to say that prior to the amendment proposed by the minister with regard to loans for farms and for the housing of the people engaged in mining and logging-three of our great primary industries-the National Housing Act was a mere copy of the procedure in the United States and in Great Britain, and had not been orientated to suit the particular Canadian need. This has now been done, and it is a very welcome advance.
Fifth, in the minister's statement with regard to the increase of the lending value under the National Housing Act, and also in the extension of the amortization period under the act, we have further evidence of improvement which will be very much welcomed.
All these particular matters can be dealt with when we come to the sections of the bill, when no doubt many hon. members will have improvements to suggest even beyond what the minister has proposed. But the point I want to make now with respect to these five important new departures in housing practice is this. All five new departures are simple; all five are practical; all five are obvious, and all five were urged from this side of the house during the last session of parliament and no doubt before that. The members of the opposition cannot take any particular credit for suggesting such obvious advances; but what we can take credit for, and what heightens my previous statement about the delay of the government in dealing with the housing problem, is that we did recognize that all these steps should have been taken immedi-

Housing Act
ately, and not a year after the close of hostilities. We urged that these steps should be taken at once, but that was not done.
The minister has made some great improvements, but of course there will be very much more to do after the present emergency has somewhat settled down. I can suggest to him three rather important things he will have to do in his capacity as the minister responsible for the housing policy of the country. First of all, we will require a real low rent housing policy. Such a term is used in the act now; we talk of moderate rent housing and low rent housing, but what we have now is not low rent housing in the sense that it caters to families in the bottom third of the income brackets.
In the second place a great programme of slum clearance will have to be developed over the years. In connection with these two subjects particularly there is real need for a settlement and a definition of the relative responsibilities of the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities with respect to housing. I urge upon the minister that he lose no time in holding conversations with the provincial governments and representatives of the municipalities so that a plan may be agreed upon for a division of responsibility which will suit all those bodies and which will give us a housing policy with as little red tape and friction as possible.
The fourth point I want to suggest to him, and this is the immediate matter I wish to bring to his attention, is that there should be at once an upward revision of the targets he has set for the construction of houses in Canada and for the provision of building materials. What has the minister said with regard to the targets for the construction of homes? He has given the immediate over-all need as 150.000. That, of course, is the emergency need. According to the James report on housing, the actual need over the next ten years, as hon. members will recall, is some 730,000 houses. Then the minister said that in the spring of 1947, despite all efforts being made by the industry this year, the situation will have deteriorated so there will be an immediate need, an emergency need, for 180,000 houses; and he gives as the five-year goal the construction of 480,000 houses. His estimate for the fiscal year 1946-47 is 60,000 new houses constructed, of which I understood him to say about 15,000 will be provided by direct government agencies and the remaining 45,000 by private builders. I want to call the attention of hon. members to the fact that if. as the minister has projected, we have 60,000 houses this year, 80,000 next year and 100,000 for the following three years
we shall still fall short of the target he mentioned in relation to that five-year period, namely 480,000 houses. So it is obvious that if we are to meet this need with anything like the speed and efficiency the Canadian people would desire, the minister will have to shoot at a higher target in the production of houses, starting this year. It might be said that the minister is being properly conservative, that he is going to do this but he does not want to disappoint the people by aiming too high. If that is so I am entirely in agreement, but I would point out to him also that not only may his estimate of the numbers which will be constructed be conservative, but in my opinion at least his estimate of the number that will be needed is also conservative. So I say to the minister, let him give the number as 60,000, but let him work for a very much larger number.
The other matter upon which I suggest he should raise his sights is in connection with the material shortage, which of course is the paramount factor in housing to-day. The other day the minister gave a picture which to my mind was designed to show how the situation was improving and how the government was contributing to that improvement. There; is no question that the government's measures, taken on April 29, have begun to bear fruit, now, and certainly we wish them well; but surely it would be wrong to suggest that the improvement in the first half of this year resulted from government action taken at the end of April. I think I can show it to be the fact that these great percentage increases in production have resulted from the natural recovery of business after the end of the war, from a very low total production during the war years when, as the minister has said, the material, the men and the effort were being put to other uses. Just to give that comment some point I want to refer to some of the figures mentioned by the minister. At page 3675 of Hansard he said:
The supply of cement and cement products is moving steadily forward. Production volume is the highest since 1931. ... By May, 1946, the monthly production had again increased so as to raise the per annum volume to a figure somewhat over 10,000,000 barrels.
That sounds very good, and it is very good; but I want to call the attention of the house to the fact that according to the figures of the dominion bureau of statistics, in 1929, Canada's production of cement was twelve and a quarter million barrels, so we have yet some distance to go to catch up to our production in a good year-but seventeen years ago.
Again the minister spoke about great percentage increases in the manufacture of brick. According to the figures of the dominion bur-
Housing Act

eau of statistics I find that the present average monthly brick production is almost identical with that of 1945; that there has been no actual increase in the average monthly production as between 1945 and 1946. I find, too, that Canada's production of brick in 1945, and the way it is running now, is less than half the brick production in 1929.
The minister referred to the increase in the supply of wire nails, There again I find the production is no better than 1943, which appears to have been one of our highest years.
The minister referred to an improvement in the production of structural tile. In 1929 we produced 221,300 tons of this product, while in 1945 we produced only 94,244. In 1929 we produced 307,400 square feet of floor tile, while in 1945 the production was only 197,164. In 1929 we produced, in thousands, 35,077 roofing tile, whereas in 1945 none was produced. For the first five months of 1946 the figures for structural and floor tile, which are lumped together in tons by the bureau of statistics, show a production running at the rate of
120,000	tons a year, or well under half of the production in 1929.
I mention these figures not by way of criticism of the minister, but in an effort to place in true iperspective the statement he made the other day, and to urge him-if he requires any urging-to go after this problem in a bigger way, a way of which he is capable, and not to be satisfied with the progress he indicated in his speech.
I turn now to the problem of increasing supply of building materials. At page 3674 of Hansard the minister said:
Extra cosits may be involved in obtaining increased output and, if so, the government is prepared to consider meeting these costs. Where plant expansion is necessary to eliminate materials bottlenecks, the method used to stimulate expansion of war plants will be made available.
I would make two comments on that statement, the first that again it is a year late, and the second that it is in the identical words, I believe, and certainly in the same sense, as the speech made by the minister in April to the Canadian club in Toronto. The house will notice that the earlier statement and the more recent one are both couched in the future tense, and do not indicate that any great progress has been made in dealing with extra costs, or with other problems which have been, troubling the building materials industry.
The minister insisted the other day that price ceilings are not hampering production of building materials in Canada. At that time I attempted to indicate, offhand and from memory-I had no material in front of me- one way in which the production of one type

of building material, namely lath, was being hampered by the price ceiling. Since that time I have received a report of a committee set up to deal with lumber prices and distribution in secondary industry and retail yards in Vancouver, This report is dated July 12, and a copy was sent to the minister. The whole report deals with the effect of price ceilings on the production of various articles which these lumber yards and secondary woodworking industries manufacture in Vancouver. If the minister will consult his copy, I believe he will find an answer to the problem he put to me.
One of the specific articles entering into the construction of houses, which is mentioned in the report, and the production of which is allegedly being held back by the illogical price ceilings in force with respect to these products, is fir flooring. It is stated that the retail price ceiling of flooring, when manufactured is less than the price ceiling on the flitches from which it is manufactured. Doors are almost unobtainable, and the reason given is the price ceiling. A similar condition exists with respect to lath, to which I referred the other day.
I do not wish to read in detail from the report, but in the section dealing with milit-work operations they say:
The millwork factories, generally speaking, state that they are unable to make long-distance plans unless the prices board will state its policy in regard to increases in prices of material and labour.
And again:
In regard to doors, the prices at present authorized result in very few doors being made.
In the summary of the report one finds certain rather significant statements, in these words:
The two most troublesome matters with which industry has to deal are the diota of the prices board:
(a)	That industry must absorb increased labour costs without price relief unless financial distress is shown.
(b)	That price increases cannot be granted on single items or groups of items if over-tall profit is satisfactory.
In addition, the members of the committee find a distressing lack of knowledge as to what the policies of the prices board are; which prevents long distance planning and reduces business almost to a day to day venture.
And again:
No firm faced with rising costs is willing to institute any long distance manufacturing plan based on past results. Manufacturers can only concern themselves with the conditions here present, and they state that unless the prices board can be more realistic they are unable to swing into full production.
Concerning the suggestion that firms must manufacture loss items if the all-over profit

Housing Act
position is satisfactory, the plain facts are that only in a few cases are these loss items continued in production.
That will give some indication of the views of this body, at least, as to the effect of price ceilings on the production, of goods needed in house building. I would ask the minister when we reach the committee stage to indicate in greater detail what he is going to do to help the industry produce more building material. If the minister is right, and if price ceilings are not hampering maximum production, then what does he mean by the promise that the government will meet extra costs involved? Does that mean an increase in the price ceiling? Does it mean subsidies? What does it mean?
To my mind we must remember that we in Canada have faith in a free enterprise economy. Surely with the shortage of materials and houses the minister has shown, there should be the greatest possible challenge to private enterprise, to free enterprise. Under normal circumstances private enterprise should have no difficulty in meeting that challenge and getting after production without any great help from the government. In my view private enterprise in most respects is capable of doing this job and standing on its own feet. When the minister speaks of assisting with extra costs, I should like to know whether he means subsidies or price increases. The policy with regard to price controls on imported goods has recently been changed. I am wondering if before that policy was changed there was a lessening of importations into Canada of such items as glass and electrical equipment required in the building of houses, which are two items that we must necessarily import. One other difficulty which faces private enterprise in its efforts to meet this problem may be the necessity of obtaining quotas from the minister before they can go into production. Then again sometimes they cannot get the machinery necessary to set themselves up in business.
The minister has properly lamented over the strikes and work stoppages that have occurred. Is this not a problem for government labour policy? Should there not be a policy that would prevent these strikes and that would satisfy the various partners in industry? The government cannot just say that the strikes have occurred, and then wash its hands of responsibility for their effect upon the production of building material.
The minister spoke of assistance to building material producers by Way of double depreciation. Does that mean that the taxation policy of this government is going to hamper production? The minister spoke also
of a labour shortage. I will go all the way with him when he talks about the lack of skilled tradesmen and the necessity of our developing a skilled working force in the country, but what about the people who are already trained and working? Is the taxation policy of this government such that those people are willing to work and produce to the maximum of their capabilities, or is that taxation policy hampering production?
One does not hear a great deal about extra shifts, certainly not in the part of the country from which I come. I am told that the reason why there are no extra shifts being worked in the mills is a lack of logs. What can be done now that the lumber strike has been settled to get more and more men into the woods so that we can have extra shifts and increase the supply of lumber for the home market?
I should not criticize the government like this without admitting wholeheartedly that there is one factor for which the government cannot be held responsible. I refer to the shortage of materials and work stoppages in connection with the production of materials that are imported from outside Canada. I realize the serious effect that this has had upon the minister's efforts to increase production.
However, I contend that the solution of this whole problem is the government's ultimate responsibility. The reason it is not being solved faster is that which was given so regretfully by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. After referring to the size of our national income and the amount of money we were making, he expressed regret that he did not see in the country that cooperation toward a single end which would make all things possible for us in Canada. If we' could get that happy cooperation toward a single end, many of the minister's problems with regard to the production of materials and houses would be solved. It is the responsibility of this government to see that policies are put into effect which will obtain that cooperation. After all, that is the ultimate purpose of any government.
The last thing I should like to refer to is the increase in the lending value, which the minister has said will be ten per cent. This will bring the lending value up from 135 per cent to 145 or 150 per cent of 1939 prices. The minister went on at some length to explain why no other increase was possible. If, as he says, the figure of 150 per cent closely represents the additional cost of home building from 1939 to 1946, I should have no great complaint to make. But I have some figures here which I obtained from a Vancouver
Housing Act

paper and which suggest to me that the percentage of increase over 1939 costs is much greater. If I am right, then the ten per cent increase will not do any good.
My figures deal with a house 1,000 square feet in size, built on a lot costing 1500. With the lot at $500 and a 1,000 square foot house, the National Housing Act figure of $4.20 per square foot would give a total lending value of $4,700. The loan which would be granted under the act would be $4,100. The cost of construction is taken at $6 per square foot, which would make this house of 1,000 square feet cost $6,500. The owner would have to contribute $2,300 out of the total cost of $6,500, which means that he would be contributing about thirty-three per cent as a down payment. That makes it most difficult for many people to build houses.
The minister has announced a ten per cent increase. Using the same house as an illustration, and taking a similar lot costing $500, we find that the lending value on the basis of $4.62 a square foot amounts to $5,120. The loan which would be granted would be $4,384. The cost is still $6,500, and the amount the individual must put up in order to build the house is $2,116. The total saving to the person who wishes to put up a house is $184, or let us say $200 out of a total investment or a total down payment of $2,300. I suggest to the minister that that is not adequate relief. If my figures of $6 per square foot for the actual cost and the figures given by the National Housing Act authorities of $4.20 and $4.62 are accurate, they would suggest a need of further revision. I suggest to the minister that he try to raise the lending value to something more closely approximating the total cost.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO LOAN PROVISIONS-CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few general remarks on the housing act and the housing policy, especially as they affect British Columbia. I have no apologies to make for speaking from the provincial point of view, because this policy is of special importance in British Columbia-not just because the difficulties of our housing problem in Vancouver are much more aggravated than in any other part of Canada, but because lumber is the basis of housing, and lumber is the real basis of our industrial economy in British Columbia.
Vancouver has long been the timber capital of Canada; indeed, it is one of the great timber centres of the world. The people in the Vancouver area have always' been used to having cheap lumber in plentiful supply. So to-day when lumber is in short supply, at

least to the private builder and to the vetqran in the Vancouver area, you can understand why the irritation over the present housing policy is perhaps greater there than it is anywhere else in Canada. When I was at home at Easter, which is one of the few chances a western member gets to visit his constituents during the session, I visited the operators of the saw mills in my riding, which includes the greatest number of saw mills in any riding in Canada. I also visited what was left of the retail lumber yards in the Vancouver area, and also a number of building contractors, and discussed this problem with them. I found, to my surprise, that there is no lumber shortage in Canada to-day. The shortage is not in the production of lumber. It is the improper and inadequate distribution of the lumber that is being cut that is causing the trouble. I want to give a few brief figures to illustrate this point. This year we expect the greatest cut in Canada's history, roughly five billion feet of timber.

Yes, and when, these big saw mills go into the retail trade they have not the facilities that the small yard has. The price of labour in the British Columbia lumber industry is the highest in Canada. The big contractor who is building a factory or a baseball stadium wants hundreds of thousands of feet of lumber, with say fifty thousand feet of two by fours. In the lumber yards lumber is stocked in sling loads, 2.000 feet in, a stack, which can be lifted on a truck as a unit. It is no bother for the saw mill to sell to such a buyer, who simply lifts the stack on to his truck. However when the veteran goes to the mill with a requisition for 10,000 or 12,000 feet, four pages of typewritten requisitions for different types of lumber, so much flooring, so much sheeting, so much joists, wall board, shingles, and all the rest, the saw mill has not sufficient labour to go running around the yards to sort out fifty feet here, a hundred feet there, five hundred feet there, and so on, to fill the veteran's order. So it is the big contractor who is getting the bulk of the lumber produced in the Vancouver area to-day, simply because the saw mills are trying to cut their losses. He is engaged perhaps on a big-time housing project but also in building moving picture theatres, baseball stands, barbecues and all the rest.
The saw mills which were in business before the war are still selling their quotas to the retail outlets, but there has been a great change in the ownership of the saw mills. Buyers from the east have come in, even brewers, who saw that the lumber trade was going to be profitable in, time of war. The result is that many of the mills have changed hands and then have broken off the relations the mill had with the retail outlets, and as the hon. .member for Vancouver South, has said, many of the retail lumber yards are closed as a consequence. They are trying to stay in business by selling anything which comes to them-cement which they cannot get, nails which they cann-ot get, paint, tiles, and so
39S4
Housing Act

on but they have not got lumber. Because of that the small builder and the veteran who are seeking small orders of lumber are having a very difficult job to get it.
One other thing I must say in support of the pre-war saw mill operators. 'Last year a movement was started by Mr. King of the King Mills to make building supplies available for veterans, entirely aside from any government priorities. Through his efforts, a movement was started amongst the mills which provided lumber for 1,200 veterans' houses last year in the Vancouver area. The great weakness, therefore, as I pointed out, as far as British Columbia is concerned, is in distribution, the fact that because of being forced to sell at below the cost of production without any sort of subsidy, the mills are naturally trying to cut that loss as far as possible by selling retail in large quantities, and at the expense of the small builder who cannot get lumber.
I come back to the lumber yard in the Vancouver area. The Minister of Reconstruction made the comment that he thought the retail lumber yards were doing very well out of this present emergency; and I agree that they are, in the east, but not in Vancouver. I want to	give you	some	figureswhich one operator	gave me	when	I	wasvisiting him. He had an order for 50,000 feet of structural timber, 12 x 12 and 16 x 10, from eastern Canada, He got $26 per thousand, wholesale price loaded in the railway cars. It was taken to Montreal at a freight cost of $29 per thousand, or a total cost of $55 per thousand. This of course was consigned to a retail	yard, in Montreal,	andall this man had to	do was to	pick	up	the
phone and tell the construction company their timbers were at the siding and the construction company picked it up. The retailer got $84 a thousand, or $29 net profit, $3 more per thousand than the logger got for logging and sawing the timber. The retail yards in British Columbia think they have a real cause of complaint; for on a similar deal in British Columbia they would get nothing. The small builder in British Columbia feels that he has an even greater cause of complaint.
The next point is the priority system. I agree with the hon. member for St. Paul's that this business of having the cities issue priorities is not working out. I am convinced that we should not have priorities laid down on a hard and fast national basis, but I do believe that the award of priorities should be on a regional basis. He used the example, I think, of the city of Toronto having no control over priorities in Mimico. I might take my own district of Vancouver. The city

council of Vancouver have no authority over priorities issued in North Vancouver or in New Westminster. So if some enterprising business man comes from the east to 'build a factory, and finds that he cannot get a timber priority from the city of Vancouver, he will go to North Vancouver or to New Westminster-New Westminster will invite him there-and they get the industry but the lumber comes out of the local domestic supply. The situation involves local pressures on local aldermen as well'. It would be better if we had a regional system from, say, 'Chilliwack to Vancouver and West Vancouver to Ladner, and some system of priorities laid down within that area.

speechtext: Would it not be better to get rid of the priorities altogether?

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO LOAN PROVISIONS-CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION
speechtext:
No, I would not get rid of the priorities altogether. I am convinced, speaking as a veteran, that a veteran's priority could be properly worked in that area. The sawmill people themselves showed it could work with those 1,200 veterans' houses which they supplied lumber for last year. Veterans and small builders would be encouraged to go ahead and build houses, and I am convinced that it is the small builder who is going to build houses in this country, not the large construction companies, formerly in heavy construction, who are in the housing business for money.
I want to summarize the effect of this policy on various individuals. First, on the small builder who cannot get lumber. He scrapes around from mill to mill. In the Vancouver area each mill makes something different; and he goes from one mill to another in search of lath, flooring, pine for wallboards, and shingles. During this time the house is standing idle. The rains come-and we have rain out there. He has to continue paying his help. As the minister has pointed out, we are short of carpenters, plasterers and bricklayers, and unless he continues to pay them, even when they are idle for lack of money, one of the big companies who are getting lumber will employ them, and so his costs will mount. So this $15 below the cost of production is no boon to the small builder since he can't get the lumber. One contractor who has an enviable business in West Vancouver told me that this business of shopping around to all mills within forty miles of Vancouver for lumber formerly assembled by local yards costs him a minimum of $30 per thousand more than the cost price of the lumber.
Now I am going to recapitulate the effects the present policy has in British Columbia, first on the retail lumber yards in Vancouver.

Housing Act
Most of these, except those fortunate ones who are dealing with mills still in the hands of the pre-war owners, have been driven out of the lumber business; they are trying to sell paint, nails, wallboard, cement, et cetera, hoping they will last out until conditions become normal again. We are always going to need, even in the Vancouver area, good active retail lumber yards, just as we need in this country retail outlet of every description; and the responsible saw mill operators who have been in the business for years gone by, and who intend to remain in the business for years ahead, are the very ones who realize that most strongly.
Now I want to speak, secondly, of the effect on the British Columbia timber industry- and that is the worst effect of all. Timber is and has been and will be the very bedrock of our British Columbia economy. One-third of the people in British Columbia earn their bread and butter directly from the timber trade, and I think most of the rest of us earn it indirectly. Members from the west and the maritimes have spoken here, of course, again and again and again of how the trade policy of this country is determined down here for Ontario and Quebec; that has certainly been true of our timber industry. We have had to go abroad to seek markets for British Columbia lumber. Before the war we did not sell any British Columbia lumber to speak of-apart from a little of the big dimension construction timber,-here in the east, or on the prairies, except clear finishing stuff, because the prairies have quite a good saw mill industry. Apart from what we sold in the British Columbia market we sold clears to the prairie market and some structural timber to the eastern market, and to sell the rest we had to go out in the markets of the world-and when I say "we" I mean the provincial government and the industry itself. It is a well-organized and highly developed industry. They built up their trade routes and made their own contacts. Our people competed with high quality and low price against Russian and Baltic timber in Britain, in spite of the very long haul from Vancouver, and also obtained markets in South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, and even in the United States. And now government policy is forcing us to ruin deliberately that entire long, slow, difficult and entirely provincial development of our world trade, because we are being forced to sell at far below the cost of production here on the domestic market, and told to recoup it by charging exorbitant prices-the timber trade would be the first to admit it-in the export market. The effect in the future will be that the people of Canada will expect British
Columbia timber to be sold at less than the cost of production. Eastern lumber is being sold retail here at, for example, $60 per thousand, while $36 retail is the domestic price as far as British Columbia is concerned. The effect on our export markets is obvious; and in British Columbia we lived in the past, live now and are going to have to live in the future, on export markets. Yet we are being driven out of our painfully established prewar export markets by the very tactics which this government refuses to condone as far as wheat is concerned. If we proposed to go on world markets with our wheat to-day and charge all the market would bear $3, $4, $5 a bushel, in order to sell our wheat cheaply at home for a dollar or less, you know the screams which would go up from the prairie members on this side, and the even louder screams from prairie members on the opposition side. Yet that is the policy which is being followed in regard to British Columbia lumber. Quite true, it is to alleviate a national housing emergency, but even the present emergency does not demand a course that will ruin British Columbia's primary economy, and that is exactly what this policy is doing.
Now as to the present allocation of markets. Fifty per cent local; and no one would dispute the allocation of thirty-five per cent to Britain: we are for that, because Britain was our best and surest pre-war market, despite Baltic competition. There remains the fifteen per cent which at present is being broken down, ten per cent to Australia, New Zealand and other British dependencies and dominions, and five per cent to the United States. On that fifteen per cent we are expected to recoup the losses made selling fifty per cent domestically at a loss of $15 a thousand, and we cannot do it without charging export prices which will ruin any hope of keeping these markets in the 3'ears ahead.
One other thing as far as the timber trade in British Columbia is concerned. You all know of the recent wage increase which has been granted of fifteen cents an hour. It is being used as a pattern by the unions across Canada in their present demands and it has put the British Columbia industry, including the operators and the workers, in an even more difficult position to maintain production under present price policy. I would suggest certain remedies, and I do so realizing that the price ceiling must be maintained. I represent a labour riding, and realize that it is unpopular in British Columbia to suggest that prices, and especially timber prices, be raised; but despite this I suggest first of all that the price of domestic British Columbia lumber be
Housing Act

raised $15 a thousand, so that at least the industry will be given a chance to sell at cost of production and not at loss. That would enable them to scale down a little their prices to our export trade. It would be still $10 less than the domestic price of eastern lumber.
Second, I think there should be a control reinstituted on the price of logs. When the ceiling was taken off logs the price went up $6, and the saw mills who did not own their own logging operations were squeezed, buying at $25 and trying to sell lumber at $26. I am afraid that if an increase were given to the saw mill operators on lumber without a control being reimposed on logging, once again you would have the loggers putting up the price of logs almost to a level with the price of lumber. That would not affect the big operators, H. R. MacMillan, Fraser Mills and the new British Columbia Products, who log their own timber. But the small operators and saw mills in the Vancouver area who buy from logging operators would be in just as difficult a position as they are at present.
Third-and this is most important to all the small builders in Vancouver-with that price the government should insist on every mill in the Vancouver area sending a high quota, as high as in peace time, to the retail yards, so that any man wanting to build a house could go to the retail yard as he could in peace time and get his lumber-because there is sufficient lumber on the market if available for proper distribution. Such a policy would actually save the builder money in British Columbia. He would have to pay $15 a thousand more on a ten thousand foot or five-roomed house, which would cost him $150 more; but on that estimate, which my contracting friend gave me of $30 a thousand extra cost to-day because of the present delays, and the time and difficulties involved in hawking around the saw mills trying to get fifty feet of lumber here and a thousand there, exposure of the unfinished house to the elements, the cost of having to keep men in employment without having work for them to do, and paying them-all these difficulties and inconveniences would be removed if the retail yards were given their proper quotas so that if the builder wanted lumber he could get what he wanted, no matter how small an order and all from one source. The net effect would therefore be to save the small builder $15 a thousand on his costs.
Lastly, I suggest that the system of priorities be put on a regional basis so that there will not be competition between adjoining towns, one town decently trying to carry out

the present emergent housing policy while another town looks to the future, desiring industries, and giving priorities for lumber to factories, theatres, shops, athletic stands and the like, lumber which should be used for housing. Only when these priorities are put on a regional basis, embracing a region which is more or less an economic unit, can there be satisfaction in the matter of priorities.
