Mr. Speaker, I need not say that we all consider the present housing conditions in Canada as most critical; as a matter of fact some have even gone so far as to say that it is bordering on a disgraceful state of affairs. For a nation with such unlimited resources and at the moment, as in the past, idle man-power, there is positively no excuse for a shortage of houses. There has always been a housing shortage, so the war cannot be blamed entirely for the present deplorable lack of living accommodation. It is not a temporary condition, though it is particularly bad at the present moment. This is just another unpleasant result of capitalistic policies. People have moved from rural areas throughout the country to crowd out our urban centres. This has been going on for decades. In 1871, according to the Canada Year Book, our rural population was 80 per cent of the total population of the country. By 1941 the number of people living in rural areas had decreased to just under 45 per cent of our total population. The development of large overpopulated urban centres, at the cost of a depleted rural population, is a situation to be deplored; for a nation's strength always lies in its rural folk. It indicates that a most unsatisfactory economic situation existed in the rural areas; and for that matter, Mr. Speaker, it still exists or people would not be continually migrating to the larger centres of population.
Large industries located in our cities are taking a disproportionate share of the wealth of the nation, leaving rural districts on the whole in an impoverished state. As a result of the removal of wealth from the rural areas, housing generally there is at a very low standard. On the other hand workers flock to the cities to operate private enterprise. The wealth in our urban centres is concentrated in a few hands, with the result that thousands of workers are inadequately housed. They are paid low wages and thus cannot afford to provide themselves with houses of their own,

Housing Act
or even to pay rentals that would provide decent housing accommodation. According to the Curtis report, in 1941 one-third of Canada's population lived in the metropolitan areas of twelve cities in Canada. In these specific areas 63-6 per cent, or almosit two-thirds of the population were tenants living on incomes too small to enable them to purchase houses of their own. Of this group only one-third had incomes of $1,800 per year or more. An}mne should know that incomes below this amount are insufficient to permit people to buy or build their own dwellings.
It seems obvious, then, that unless the incomes of these people are increased the government must evolve some system of subsidized housing in order to provide these folk with decent living quarters. There is no subsidized housing in Canada as there is in the United Kingdom or New Zealand or even the United States. The few houses provided on small holdings under the Veterans Land Act or by Wartime Housing Enterprises represent a weak-hearted attempt to meet an almost hopeless situation; and because of this crisis in housing, what do we find? Three and four and five families living in dwellings only large enough to house one family decently. I need hardly say that such overcrowding breeds delinquency among children and creates a generally unwholesome atmosphere everywhere. This shortage of houses existed before the war, as was freely admitted by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) in his address on housing last Monday. The war aggravated an almost intolerable situation. Lack of construction during the war years and the accelerated movement of people from rural to urban areas to work in munition plants contributed to the crisis in housing we face to-day; and the veteran returning to Canada has to face that situation.
To say that similar conditions exist elsewhere is to beg the question. Canada has the material for construction; she has the man-power for it; but the programme thus far outlined by the government is woefully inadequate. The veteran is the forgotten man as far as housing in urban centres is concerned. Even in rural and suburban areas, projects for veterans have to wait because of shortages of building materials, shortages caused by the lack of any provision in our statutes prohibiting the erection of theatres, garages, filling stations and luxury homes throughout the country. Veterans do without, while materials are being used in non-essential building. Ceilings should have been imposed upon house building, as has been done in the United Kingdom. Until the present crisis is relieved, the construction cost
of houses should be limited to $7,000; and until veterans are provided with houses a regulation should be invoked giving priorities to veterans only for house building. Luxury houses can wait until veterans secure shelter for their families. I am certain this nation does not want men who fought for our way of life to be homeless. Nothing to-day is more important in my opinion than the provision of houses for the boys who fought for democracy.
Besides the difficulty of obtaining materials, the veteran is faced with inflated prices. To finance a pre-war modest home of $3,600 now requires $5,000 or more. The government provides little assistance to the veteran in securing a building loan at a low rate of interest. National housing provides only a portion of the money he requires for financing his dwelling, and at 4J per cent interest. No preference is given to the veteran over the civilian. An interest rate of 2J per cent might well have been provided as a maximum. The government could well have absorbed the difference between 2J per cent and the 4J per cent which is charged to civilians. This would in small measure meet the inflated prices with which the veteran is faced in the purchase of construction materials-inflated prices which in most cases developed while he was in uniform serving his country. He was unable to provide a home for his family, as most civilians here in Canada were able to do when they saw prices of construction products rising.
The government provides ex-servicemen with a few hundred dollars as a civil reestablishment credit, to assist them to provide accommodation for themselves and their families. With the inflated building costs and high prices for houses, this is only a drop in the bucket. The move was a commendable one as far as it went. The credit looked big to the soldier when he served on European frontiers, but when he endeavours to locate a house to-day it looks pathetically small.
Even second rate houses have advanced in price 50 per cent to 100 per cent. Veterans canniot hope to pay these excessive prices. Indeed it is anything but fair for a grateful country to expect them to pay those exorbitant prices. Long 'ago a ceiling should have been placed on the prices of houses. Ceilings have been placed on other commodities; why not on houses? They need not be selling at such unreasonable prices. I appeal to the government to do that at once.
During the war the wartime prices and trade board' placed a ceiling on rentals. This was an attempt to control rates which in many cases had become excessively high. It was for the most part successful-perhaps every-
Housing Act

where except in the city of Ottawa, where some of us had to pay as high as $35 for one room. Nevertheless it was a step in the right direction. But no attempt has been made to control prices in house sales. Speculators and real estate dealers have been allowed to make a killing at the cost of the veteran. By allowing prices of houses to sky-rocket, and prices in general to run wild, the government has defeated the purpose for which the civil reestablishment credit was set up.
Prices have reached prohibitive heights. It has been a field day for private speculators. It is not fair to the boys who were seeking a place in which to live; it is unfair to the buying public at large. People have made enormous profits by selling homes to veterans scarred by war. Veterans have been forced to pay fantastic prices in order to obtain shelter for their families. This sort of thing should have been stopped long ago. Ceiling prices should have been placed upon these houses. It is not yet too late to rectify that error. If rental controls could be made to work, surely ceiling price controls could be made effective on housing.
It has been suggested that this type of control would be difficult to establish. I am not so sure about that. Has it been tried? I am satisfied that controls could be based, first, upon location-whether houses are urban or rural; second, upon the size and number of rooms; third, on the type of house, whether modern, semi-modern, or unequipped; and, fourth, upon age. I ask the government now to remedy this situation, which is working to the detriment of almost every married veteran in Canada.
There is a dearth of low-rental homes throughout the country. The bill before the house will not provide low-priced housing and therefore will not provide low-rental housing. Subsidized housing is the only answer to the problem. Private enterprise has never met this situation and is not meeting it to-day. It has failed miserably. The Canadian Legion is cognizant of the true situation. In the Ottawa Journal of July 19 the following appears;
The "primary need" in the national housing emergency is to provide low-rental'homes for war veterans, Major Gen. C. B. Price, of Montreal, president of the Canadian Legion's Dominion Command, said in an address at a luncheon meeting of the Dominion Construction Association management committee here yesterday.
A "good many" married veterans in low income brackets were "terribly discouraged" because all their efforts "to secure decent living accommodation, for their families, at anything like the rentals they can afford to pay, had been of no avail."
It was "nothing short of deplorable" that the veterans' chances of success in reestablishment

in civilian life were "far less than they otherwise would be, due to the constant strain of anxiety on the score of living accommodation."
Gen. Price appealed for the association's cooperation both in obtaining low-cost housing and in helping veterans reestablish themselves in building trades.
The only "practical relief" so far provided veterans seeking low-rent accommodation has been through Wartime Housing Limited, and the only satisfactory solution to the emergency was in making more subsidized housing units available to low income veterans, he said.
"Not nearly enough" had been done to ease the veterans' housing problem and veterans should be given a "right of way over all other house building activities."
In conclusion I wish to emphasize again these points:
(1)	The shortage of building materials could be substantially relieved by banning nonessential building.
(2)	Materials would go further if restrictions were placed on the erection of dwellings exceeding $7,000 in value.
(3)	A building loan should be provided veterans at a lower rate of interest than is charged under National Housing, to enable them to meet the high costs now prevailing.
(4)	A priority should be set up for veterans for home building.
(5)	A ceiling should be placed on selling prices of houses as a temporary expedient to enable the veteran to secure housing at a reasonable cost.
(6)	A subsidized housing programme should be set up by the government to meet the demand for low-rental housing.
The veterans are not receiving a square deal to-day in the matter of housing. All they ask is a square deal and nothing more. I believe that if the suggestions I have made are acted upon by the government, more and cheaper housing can be provided.
This country must provide housing for its ex-service personnel at reasonable cost, and the public would support any move on the part of the government to meet that situation. As Theodlore Roosevelt said, a man who is good enough to shed his blood for his country is good enough to be given a square deal; more than that no man is entitled to, and less than that no man shall have. Let us give our veterans a square deal in housing. They ask for nothing more, and to that at least they are entitled.

Ordinarily questions and answers come at the committee stage. All I can say is that Wartime Housing has built certain projects with basements and other projects *without basements, and it has been found necessary to charge $7 a month more for a house with a basement than for one without a basement, in each case the computation being on the same basis. I think if my hon. friend undertook to put a cellar under his house for $256 he will find that he is very optimistic and is likely to be severely disappointed.

I know I have the right figure for the cost of the blocks, and I am sure I am allowing enough for wages for two men to lay the blocks in two days.
Mr. ALISTAIR STEWART (Winnipeg
North): Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) is going to have a rather rough time with this bill, and yet I should like him to know that we all realize the magnitude of the problem which he has inherited, and that we want to see that problem solved. However, I feel quite certain that it will not be solved on the basis of the statement which the right hon. gentleman made to this house last week. It was a frank statement; it was an honest statement, interspersed with occasional dashes of the minister's insuperable optimism. He told us that the deficit confronting the country was approximately 180,000 houses, but it is really much greater than that. Were the people of Canada to be properly housed we should; have to build anything between 700,000 and 1,000,000 more houses.
The minister has told us that it is the intention of the government to build another 480,000 houses by March, 1952, and that private enterprise is being depended upon to build them. I state quite categorically that private enterprise, I do not care how much it is assisted by the government, will not build that number of houses in this country by 1952. The aspiration is laudable; we should like to see these houses built, but I think we know from experience in the past in Canada, and from the experience of other countries, that private enterprise is not capable of handling the housing problem in a country such as ours, and the minister has said that that problem is rapidly worsening. He should know by now, from the deputations which have waited upon the government, from resolutions passed by municipalities, and from statements which have emanated from commissions of inquiry, that private enterprise cannot build these houses. If he is dissatisfied with the statements of groups outside of the government I will quote him part of pamphlet No. 21, issued as long ago as 193S by the Department of Pensions and National Health at Ottawa, as follows:
We need dwellings for the lowest income groups who have not, and may never have the ability or opportunity to earn sufficient to pay a self-supporting rent for the size of dwelling required to house their families under minimum permissible conditions of sanitation and decency. The construction of such dwelling accommodation obviously will never be undertaken as a commercial venture by private initiative. These people need to be assisted by the community, and the manner of this assistance is the housing problem in its thorniest aspect. Almost altogether this group is a class of renters, both due to limited finances, and to their necessity to be free to move in accordance with the location of their employment.
The officials of the government have been aware for many years that private enterprise cannot solve the problem of housing for the people of Canada. Private enterprise will invest money only in the type of construction from which it can make a profit, and there is no profit in building houses for the people in this country who need them most, the submerged third who must have houses which rent at from $10 to $16 a month. Private enterprise will erect the buildings we have been hearing about-theatres, garages, filling stations, and so on. I was in Montreal and I saw the foundation being laid for a new hotel of 1,100 bedrooms. I do not say for one moment that Montreal does not need another hotel, but I do say that if Montreal has got along for the last two or three years without another hotel they should be able to get along for the next two or three years
Housing Act

and permit the plumbing supplies which will be used in the hotel to be made available for houses for veterans.
Once we solve the problem of slum conditions in Canada; once we solve the housing problem of those in the lower third of the income brackets, then we shall have solved the problem of housing. I think it is just as clear and plain as that. Yet the minister tells us that Housing Enterprises is building houses which will rent at from $39 to $45 per month for four or five rooms. Such rentals are completely outside the capacity of the ordinary wage earner to pay. These dwellings are all right for the white collar worker or the person who has an income of $2,400 or $3,000 a year, but such rentals cannot be paid by the majority of the people.
I was sorry to see-I hope I am not doing the minister an injustice-that the minister anticipates that the rentals of Wartime Housing units may be raised because the municipalities want additional taxes. A six-room wartime house rents for $30. According to the Curtis report the rental paid by a family of low income should be 20 per cent of the family income. A rental of $30 presupposes an income of $150. The great majority of the workers in my constituency who are now in wartime houses are not earning as much as $150, and the additional overhead of $2.50 for local taxes is going to bear heavily upon them.
But most unfortunate of all was the minister's statement at page 3688 of Hansard that slum clearance is considered to be inopportune at the present time. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the right hon. gentleman does not appreciate the housing conditions in Canada if he believes that. I will admit that there are psychological maladjustments which will occur when people double up in houses. They are dangerous, and socially regrettable, if you like, but they are not nearly as serious as the problems confronting those who are to-day living in slum houses, whose bodies and minds are being warped by the wretched conditions under which they live. I should like to think that an attempt to clear slums would be carried out concurrently with whatever else the minister has in mind.
The minister also mentioned at page 3691 of Hansard certain principles which were actuating the government. One I have already mentioned, the dependence on private enterprise. Private enterprise will never solve the housing problem of Canada; I say again dogmatically, it cannot do it. It has done it in no other country I know of. The only solution is for the government to tackle the problem and solve it.

The _ minister also states-and this is interesting:
If, however, with all the assistance we can provide for financing, materials and labour supply, the houses required to substantially improve the housing standard of the Canadian people are not forthcoming, then the dominion
overnment will take a direct position in the
ousing field.
That I feel, sir, is a shadow perhaps of things to come. But it is unfortunate that the government has not yet made up its mind that it is going into the housing field, because circumstances will compel it to do so, no matter how much it may try to dodge the issue.
Our principal housing problem in Canada is that of the submerged third, those whose incomes are under $1,200 and who can get decent housing conditions only when houses are subsidized or are built in such a way that low rentals are made available to them. Perhaps the house may think that I labour this point unduly, but the facts are on the record. The need for low rental housing is obvious to anybody who travels through the big cities or almost anywhere in urban areas.
Many of us receive pamphlets and publications from companies perhaps with an axe to grind. All of us are in receipt of the monthly bulletin I have here from the Imperial Oil company. A few months ago, in presenting their own social security plan within the company, they gave us an interesting table which shows that out of fifty persons at the age of sixty-five, four will have retirement incomes, four will be virtually penniless but able to work, forty-two will be without income and dependent on charity or the state. In other words, to put it into percentages, at the age of sixty-five, ninety-two per cent of our people have no incomes and no financial reserves. Surely it is obvious from that, that the people of Canada are still working with insufficient incomes.
But even more interesting and rather more specific is this quotation which I should like to give from a magazine called The Montrealer, which is distributed among the members of this house. It is an advertisement in the March issue. It is headed, "Gold is Where you Find it," and it says:
One section of Montreal, about fourteen miles square, is unique-"The gold vein" of the island.
In this area about fourteen miles square are housed some 14,000 families of this particular class, on the slopes of Mount Royal and Westmount, embracing St. George's and St. Andrew's wards, Westmount upper and lower level, Notre Dame de Grace, Hampstead, Montreal West and South, and Outre-

Housing Act
mont. The advertisement goes on to pose the rhetorical question: How does "the gold vein" live? It proceeds to inform us how the gold vein lives. It says:
"THE ACTIVE" constitutes the younger element

the offspring of "The inactive"-junior executives, the junior clubmen of town, their young wives, the debs and subdebs of town, young ladies of affairs.
I have no idea what sort of affairs they are. It goes on:
"He" and "she" play golf, tennis, badminton and bridge. They ride, fish, hunt, ski and skate. They travel in smart sport cars. They drink and smoke and, most certainly, they entertain their friends and do it in a lavish manner.
Meanwhile Europe starves!
"He" wears flannels, golf pants, sport shirts, and his hats have to be just so. His feminine prototype is known for her smart coiffures, the very latest in perfumes and cosmetics, her enviably correct sport shoes and swanky evening gowns. Together, they buy anything the imagination can create, and there is continual competition to own it before it has been discovered even by the other alert "he's" and "she's" of "the gold vein." Quality is their criterion. They are "the people other people follow."
And "THE INACTIVE"? Never were quotation marks better placed than around that word, for it doesn't look as (though they do much more than sit and sit. But don't fool yourself! They are merely the "active" grown older, and their minds are active still and decidedly mature. At their every decision the market goes up or down a point or two. "He" and "she" wear the very finest clothes. "He" is a connoisseur of food, liquors, liqueurs and wines. "She" is interested in the newest fashions and clings to all that she found enjoyable and comfortable in the past. Both patronize the theatre and the arts, take cruises and can always be counted upon for substantial subscriptions to charity and cultural endeavours.
Those are the people of "the gold vein," Mr. Speaker, and these 14,000 people in "the gold vein" in the city of Montreal have collective incomes which are greater than the total earnings of the wage earners in the provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta. These 14,000 families have assessed incomes of almost $135,000,000. The wage earners in the provinces mentioned have incomes of almost $125,000,000. These people in "the gold vein" in the city of Montreal can afford fine houses. Where do they get the money? By exploiting the people. These are the people who to-day can still get large dividends from industry. There is no hint of inflation apparently when we are told that the dividends paid by corporations in Canada were $5,000,000 greater this month than in July of last year. But let the steelworkers ask for a minimum wage of $33 a week; that, sir, is inflation of the foulest type and must be stopped. I should be inclined to
agree with the government's policy if I saw them preventing this distribution of unearned income in Canada to these people in "the gold vein" who to-day are living so well. That is how one section of the people live- "the gold vein". But go up to the parliamentary restaurant any time and look over into the city of Hull. The Hull police department reported recently about seventy-five buildings which contained 112 dwelling units which, in turn, contained 123 families. Only six of these seventy-five buildings were habitable. Thirteen of the buildings had indoor toilets, thirty-eight of the buildings had outdoor toilets, twenty-four had none at all. These are the people we have to help, these are the people whom the government is not helping.
But I should like to speak of an area of which I have some knowledge, my own city of Winnipeg, a young city, and yet one which has slum conditions which are an eyesore and a shame, not only to Manitoba but to the Dominion of Canada as a whole-and at that our slums are not so bad as those which exist in the eastern part of Canada. According to a census taken at the beginning of this year in my constituency, in which there are some 78,000 people, there were only nine vacant houses in January; eight of them were unfit for human habitation, and one was so broken down that no one could occupy it, and indeed there were no "to let" signs out at all. I went around to some of the slum homes. We have in Winnipeg a first-class health and sanitation department, of which Doctor M. S. Lougheed and Mr. Fred C. Austin are in charge, and it it was through their kindness that I was able to see some of these slums. I had seen them before; they have not improved with keeping. I went around with an able young inspector, Mr. George Kelly. I am not going to tell parliament about all the houses I saw, but this is symptomatic of affairs as they exist. I went to one building with nineteen rooms, and there were seventeen family units living in it. It was a frame building, dilapidated and down-at-heel, rented out to one of these pestilential house farmers. As one went in the door one was almost hit physically in the face by the foul and fetid stench in which the people were living. Here was the smell of cooking, of putrifying garbage, and of human excrement. Windows were broken in almost every room, patched up here and there with burlap or with paper. There was the occasional curtain, so dirty and grimy as scarce to deserve the name of curtain. Plaster in every room was cracked, broken, stained, perhaps with rain dripping down it, more often with the desiccated bodies of vermin which had been squashed to death
Housing Act

on the walls. In most of these rooms the gas stoves were not properly working. I walked into one room where a young soldier had brought his wife that very day from hospital where she had given birth to a baby. She was heating water on a gas stove, which was leaking, to bathe the infant. The room was 14 feet by 10 feet, and they were condemned to stay there and to bring up the infant in such surroundings. In every room there was a slop pail, of course. It was used for garbage and everything else, often for lavatory purposes where there were children, because there was only one toilet in the whole building, only one bath for all these people. The beds were dirty and in many cases foul. I came across one old man lying in bed and we asked him the stock question, "Are there any vermin in here?" He said, "Hell, no, not even a bedbug would live in this place"; but he was wrong, because every time we lifted up a mattress there were colonies and clusters of these vermin just waiting for the onset of night to begin their daily meal.
It may be said, why do not these people improve their conditions? Are they so lost to all sense of decency that they want to live there? No sir, they do not want to live there, but we have conditioned them to such a state that they do live there now.
Let me quote from Mr. Austin's report. As I have said already, he is chief inspector of the division of sanitation and housing in Winnipeg. This is from a report which he read at the annual general meeting of the Canadian institute of sanitary inspectors in Toronto in May. Speaking of these areas, Mr. Austin said:
Infectious diseases spread rapidly in such areas. Offenders against the criminal code have their haunts in such areas. Juvenile delinquency rears its ugly head in such surroundings and sexual promiscuity is more or less commonplace, primarily due to the lack of privacy. Common use of inadequate plumbing fixtures is also a factor here. These all have their perpetuation, if not their origin, in the decline in the will, or wish, or ability on the part of the submerged, to overcome the handicaps of inferior accommodation, congestion of population, vermin infestation, dirty rooms and habits, general slovenliness, and the acceptance of debilitated living standards, due to a decisive breakdown in their morale. The latter is a concomitant of a debased standard of living, and to expect these people to get out of their ruts of their own accord or effort, is to expect them to raise themselves by their boot straps.
It is these people whom we have to help, it is these people whom the plan of the right hon. gentleman does not help, because as a principle he abjures subsidies, as a principle he will have nothing to do with them. He says: Let the municipalities and the provinces attend to subsidies. He is going to find out
fMr. Stewart.]
that it is financially impossible for the provinces and the municipalities to remove these sore spots from all across Canada. I should like to extend an invitation to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, and I should be quite prepared to pay the financial cost of such invitation. It would cost me six dollars and a quarter. I should like the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to find out these things for himself; I invite him to come to Winnipeg and to live in one of these hovels, and when he comes back to Ottawa his mind will be radically changed, sir, about slums and how soon they should be eradicated. I said I would give him six dollars and a quarter. He may feel that that is not' unduly generous, but his government feels it is generous enough for the old people of this country. That is the weekly allowance of an old age pensioner, and since the government asks old age pensioners to inhabit these hovels, I think it is reasonable to ask the right hon. gentleman to do the same. Out of this six dollars and a quarter he will pay $4 for rent, and from the $2.25 left he will supply himself with all the food he needs to keep body and soul together. If he is willing to undertake the experiment, I shall be very glad indeed to pay up the six dollars and a quarter.
I want to point out that there is a lot of talk in this house about economy, about saving dollars and cents. Mr. Speaker, saving dollars and cents is not nearly as important as saving human lives and human respect. That is much more important than the financial economies we can make. But, speaking to this question from ithe point of view of dollars and cents, let me remind the house of certain reports which have been made. For instance, in 1935 there was a survey and a report made to the city of Detroit housing commission which showed that in the slum areas the death rate from pneumonia was three times as high, there were five times as many crimes, six times as high an infant mortality rate, ten and a half times as high a tuberculosis death rate, and fifteen times as many criminals in a small area as compared with a normal residential area. Surely, sir, there is an extraordinary extravagance with human lives and human happiness in these slum areas. Or let me refer to the city of Cleveland, Ohio, which made a survey of a blighted area which houses 2-5 per cent of Cleveland's population, and it was found that over a ten-year period this small area had 21 per cent of the city's murders, 12 per cent of the city's cases of

tuberculosis, seven per cent of its juvenile delinquents; and eight per cent of the city's relief families.
But again let me come nearer home. Let me take my own city, where a similar survey was made in 1935 by the city health department. The department took two areas in
Winnipeg, area 1 being the Assiniboine river
north to Notre Dame avenue and Red river west to Sherbrook street, area 2 being Notre Dame avenue north to the C.P.R. tracks and Red river west to Sherbrook street including all Point Douglas. The population in the first area was 29,479, in the second area 23,246, and1 in all the rest of the city 170,292. This committee found further that the cost of social services such as police, municipal hospitals, children's aid societies, General Hospital, St. Boniface outdoor clinic, social welfare and children's bureau in area 1 was $257,000 and in area 2, $381,000, while for the rest of the city it was $612,000. If the cost of social services for areas 1 and 2 had been at the same rate per thousand1 of population as for the rest of the city, the cost would have been $189,000 instead of $638,000, thus saving the city of Winnipeg roughly $450,000 per annum. Surely no additional proof is needed to show the extravagance and wastefulness of slums in this country. We can eradicate slum areas and build) decent homes for the people and save money in the long run. That is looking at it from the financial point of view. From the human point of view we can give the people of Canada an opportunity for gracious living which they have never known before.
The right hon. gentleman's reputation stands high, and deservedly so, for what he did' in the line of production for the war effort. He can make that reputation even higher if he grasps the immensity of the problem that confronts him and realizes that it can be tackled only by the help of public funds.
It would be entirely negative were I to criticize without offering some suggestions of the type of policy which the minister should follow. In the first place, the federal parliament. I believe, eventually, will have to pass enabling legislation to which the provinces can adhere, and this legislation will contain in- it provisions for a tremendously enlarged programme of research into problems of house building in Canada. It might even go so far
as to have an experimental area where these houses could be constructed and people could live in them.
The dominion government will have to be prepared to take the responsibility to a large extent financially, even perhaps as high as ninety per cent, to provide loans to provinces and regional areas in order to wipe out these festering blots called slum areas. The federal parliament will have to make money available for low rental housing all across Canada. This is not a local problem; it is not one particular city's problem; it is a Canadian problem. I submit therefore that only the Canadian House of Commons can, tackle it adequately.
Loans which are advanced will have to be far beyond those at present envisaged. Loans should be for a minimum of at least forty-five years, and the interest rate must not be any higher than two per cent. We shall be asked, how can we afford it? If we go to the people and borrow at three per cent and lend at two per cent we shall have a financial loss. I do not think that is so. Assume for the moment that we raise a billion dollars from the Canadian people for a special housing loan -and that money would be readily forthcoming-we could lend it at two per cent. Despite the confusion which exists in the minister's statement as to whether the national income depends upon housing or housing upon the national income, I suggest that the increase in national income would be so marked that the Department of National Revenue would get back far more than the ten millions which we had apparently lost by lending the money at two per cent.
But if both houses passed enabling legislation, the provincial legislatures should also be encouraged to do the same thing, and I do not think they would require very much
Housing Act

encouragement. The provincial legislature which to-day refused to take advantage of such an offer from the federal government would not exist beyond the next election, we can be sure of that.
There should be created in the provinces, departments responsible for community planning under the jurisdiction of a cabinet minister. I should like to see the matter of housing under separate portfolio in this parliament, but I am content at present to see it in the hands of the Minister of Reconstruction. The responsibilities of these departments of community planning would include the defining of various metropolitan areas and regions within the province, so that enabling legislation might permit them to establish community planning and housing commissions in such areas. I think it is a mistake, if the government is going to go into housing, as I think it will, to deal directly with the municipalities, because they are too small. We have to deal with metropolitan areas, and, in rural areas, regional divisions. Any moneys granted should be granted to the provincial governments, who in turn would channel it down to the metropolitan housing and planning commission and the regional housing and planning commission.
Of course it is obvious that these metropolitan and regional areas could be used for other administrative purposes, such as health, education and social services. The province would enter into an agreement with the dominion government which also, I hope, would have a department of community planning and housing, with loans to enable the metropolitan and regional commissions to undertake planning for future development and redevelopment, the acquisition of land for urban and regional development and housing construction, such as community centres and so on, and rental subsidies for tenants whose income is less than $1,000 a year.
Let us remember that almost one-third of our people are in the income brackets of less than $1,200 a year. These are the people whose houses would have to be subsidized. Above that level it is possible that, with ingenuity, we may have housing schemes built so economically that we shall be able to rent houses to those earning above $1,200 a year, and rent at reasonable rates.
This department should allocate dominion loans to the various metropolitan and regional commissions with the aid of the provinces. The local government has to take an important part in this picture, because while we may keep centralized control; while we have a centralized policy, to make it work we must have decentralized administration, first through

the province and then through the regional group. It is on the level of local government that the question will be decided whether good modern housing will be provided for those who need it. It will be only with the support of the whole local community for the planning scheme that any worth while action will be taken. With the exception of the land speculator and the jerrybuilder, community planning and housing is beneficial to all. It helps the home owner by reducing taxation; for slum clearance lightens the cost of fire, police and social services, and makes property values more stable. It helps the tenant by offering a good house in a nice neighbourhood. It helps the small storekeeper by leaving more of the consumer's dollar for food, clothes and furnishings. It helps the business man by providing a planned locality for his factory, with maximum traffic advantages. We should note that it is very important that this planning be done not in the sense of individual housing units but in the sense of complete areas. Such a scheme helps the municipal governments in the metropolitan area by relieving them of the drain that slums made upon their budgets, and offering them security for the future in planned development.
I could pursue these ideas very much further, Mr. Speaker, but my time is almost gone. I only want to point out to the right hon. gentleman that facts are already available showing that private enterprise is not going to do the job he wants done. Plans are available showing precisely what the government should do and what in my opinion it will be compelled to do by force of circumstances. At the moment the government has given no appearance of facing the fact that our problem lies in the lower third of the population of this country; and until it applies itself seriously to building houses for the submerged third of our people, the government consigns itself to impotence while it condemns the Canadian people to frustration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to join in this debate for a few moments because, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) who preceded me and the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. McKay), who spoke a little earlier, I feel the time has come to speak plainly to the government about its housing policy.
During the last few years the problem of housing in this country has been very serious; yet we had on our hands the needs of the war. We in this group did our best, while pointing out the impending difficulty which

Housing Act
now confronts the country, to be constructive in our suggestions to the government and not hamper the various items of housing legislation that were brought before us. Each time we have had under consideration some new measure, or the amendment of existing legislation, we have pointed out that it was inadequate, but recognizing that at least it was an attempt to improve inefficient legislative machinery we hoped it would have some beneficial result. But now the war is over; we are thinking in terms of reconstruction and the future; and I think, as do all the members of this group, it is time to point out to the government that it has failed miserably in dealing with this problem, and that as long as its mind is set on some of the principles to which it adheres it will not solve the problem that is facing the Canadian people.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat made it clear that what we need in this country is not just a target for so many housing units per year; what we need is to tackle the whole problem of the conditions under which our people are living. I dare say some hon. members felt that my hon. friend's description of the slum conditions in the area which both he and I represent in the city of Winnipeg was, shall I say, picturesque. It was partly because of that portrayal that I felt, even though my colleague had covered the subject so well, I could not refrain from saying something at this time. It is not good enough to go on telling the people who are condemned to live in these impossible buildings that theirs is a problem which must wait until some other angles of the problem have been dealt with. I have suggested before, and I suggest again, that there is no time like the present to tackle the problem of slum clearance in some of the most disgraceful areas to be found in some of our large cities. I urge upon the minister and those under him who are dealing with this matter that even yet they give consideration to taking an area such as that along both sides of the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway which divides our two constituencies, clear out the buildings which are not fit for human habitation, and really establish in that whole area decent living conditions for the people, who incidentally are workers who produce enormously in terms of wealth for this country.
When I first rose I said if the government adheres to its present basic policy it will not get anywhere with this whole problem. I have in mind the statements the minister made, as recorded in Hansard for July 22 at
page 3690 from which page my colleague has already quoted in part. At that time the minister admitted to us that there was a real problem. He said:
That a deficit of housing will confront us for some time to come is virtually certain.
Then he went on to say:
At the same time, I can assure hon. members that no effort will be spared by my department and by the government as a whole to meet the deficit, to relieve a critical situation.
Further down on the same page he summed up the main principles underlying the aims and objects of his department, and gave this as number one:
High priority. Adequate housing for the Canadian people is one of the major tasks before us. The utmost effort will be directed towards meeting this need, and the resources of the country will be used to this end.
When one hears forthright statements of that kind one expects the government to mean them, and that nothing will stand in the way of the government's determination to get houses built to meet not only the immediate need in terms of housing units but also the need in terms of better standards of housing and the improvement of whole areas. But having said that the minister immediately went on to say, referring to his department and his government:
It is the policy to ensure that as large a portion as possible of housing be built by private initiative.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I could, but at the moment I am not going to, enter into an argument as to the respective merits of private and public housing, but it does seem to me this is the crux of the matter as far as this government is concerned. It says nothing'will be allowed to stand in the way; then immediately afterwards it says: We are fastening our flag to the mast of private enterprise. It seems to me the government needs to turn its policy right around and say: Our first concern, the first item in our policy, is to get houses built. But as one goes through the speech of the minister, and as one goes through the legislation we have before us, it becomes clear that the government's first concern is not the building of houses. The government's first concern is the maintenance of private enterprise in the field of housing. I insist that what we want is not the enunciation, first of all, of the method or the principle by means of which the end is to be achieved, but rather the determination that that end is to be achieved. The need is recognized by the minister as well as by the rest of us; for even when he gives his plausible
Housing Act

reasons for not going ahead with shun clearance he is making an admission that the problem is there.
Then, respecting the government's activity in the housing field, the minister went on to say that the government is there only because it has been forced into it. But the thing that annoys us, entirely apart from the fact that we are dealing with differences in political faiths, is that we represent a people who are sorely pressed >by these needs, and we hate to see loyalties to a way of doing things put ahead of a determination to meet actual needs.
On the next page the minister said this:
We are in these endeavours because in each instance housing of this type would not otherwise be forthcoming. We would be very happy to withdraw, but there seems no immediate prospect of housing of this type being produced by other means.
All the way through the government's attitude there runs that refrain-that they do not like being in the housing field; that they would be happy to withdraw. They want to get out as soon as possible. Again I quote from the minister's remarks:
I hope that the dominion government's direct participation in the housing field will reduce rather than increase, but we are determined to see that an adequate number of homes are built in Canada in the future.
If the minister will stand by the last half of that sentence, I shall go down the line with him, because it implies that he is willing to throw over his prior insistence that they are going to stick by private enterprise. Surely after the observations of the hon. member who has just taken his seat the house is not going to be satisfied with legislation that will leave us with a worse situation a year hence than we now have, and which does not tackle the needs of our people who are living in substandard homes and in slum areas.
Again at page 3691 the minister said this:

I am told that small mills cannot afford to produce lumber at the price that is being asked for logs. That is sufficient consideration to merit an investigation by the Department of Reconstruction, or at least by the wartime prices and trade board. If that information is correct there will only be one result, namely that the small mill will go out of business, and there will be less lumber produced at a time when Canada needs lumber more than anything else.

May I point out that all the logs which are cut are being sawed into lumber by someone. I do not think my hon. friend would suggest that the same number of logs will not be cut into lumber, or that the same amount of lumber will not be put on the market.
Logs can be held in the water for a year.
I should like to know of a concern that is holding them for a rise in price.
You could not do anything about it, if they were?
Could I not?
No, not under your present law.

Who is the timber controller, and what are his duties? Then, what are the prices of logs and rough lumber in various regions of Canada? I believe this information would be useful. I am alarmed at the concern shown by the hon. member for Vancouver South respecting the small operator, and
particularly when I think of the way in which lumber prices in my own city have risen. It seems to me that if the small operator is suffering in the transaction, then the fellow at the other end supplying the logs is receiving an inordinate share of the total price. A statement showing the amount each of these individuals receives, from the tree to the finished house, would have considerable merit in this discussion. I know that in my own city lumber has increased in price since before the war from $40 to $75 per thousand. When I think of logs being worth from $6 to $12, I am inclined to think the difference is not all taken up by freight. Could the minister give a picture of the timber control situation, with figures?
I have not the figures before me. Prices of lumber in various areas of Canada are different, having regard to the conditions in those areas.
Freight conditions?

No. The difference is largely governed by the amount of the product which goes for export. For example, on the Pacific coast the export quota was 65 per cent of the cut, this for historic reasons. The bulk of the coastal lumber has always been exported. Then, in the prairie provinces the export quota is two-fifths of the cut; in Ontario and Quebec it is one-third, and in the mari-times a different proportion.
The timber controller sees that the requirements of the home market are looked after in accordance with the formula set. He takes care of such priorities as may be issued by the director of priorities. He generally sees that the distribution of lumber conforms with the needs of the various areas in Canada. He has charge of the whole lumber programme and he functions with a staff of, I think, 300 persons. He has officers in all parts of Canada to see that the regulations are carried out.
You have not discussed the prices of materials.
Prices are such that the producer is allowed a reasonable margin of profit.
There is no ceiling on logs.

Going back for a moment to the subject the hon. member for Vancouver South was talking about, I should like to add my voice to his in asking the minister to investigate the situation in British Columbia with respect to price ceilings and the supply of lumber. It is apparent to me from what the minister has said-and I say this
Housing Act

with all respect-that he is not as familiar with the situation there as are some of us who live in Vancouver.
For instance, the minister said that the lumber yards are doing better than they have ever done in their history. I understand that that is perfectly true of those located east of the rookies, but it is not true of British Columbia where the mills are direct competitors of the lumber yards and have simply forced them out of business. In order to get a return for its cut, a mill must take the retail price fixed by the board and not just the wholesale price.
The minister suggested that the financial position of companies in British Columbia was quite satisfactory and that, therefore, no price adjustment was necessary. Where do they get that profit? We who are from British Columbia know it comes from the export trade. As the hon. member for Vancouver North said, the domestic trade is carried on at a loss of something like $15 per thousand. There is another interesting thing about the structure of this industry. The minister referred to the large capital which had been built up on the export trade. These are the mills located on the Fraser river or at Port Alberni. In the normal days of peace their domestic trade was almost nil; practically 90 per cent of their business was export. Deep sea ships would come along their wharves, load and sail without coming near Vancouver.
On the other hand, a large number of mills -these are the mills referred to in the press report mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South-are domestic mills. Many of them are located along False creek in Vancouver, or in other cities and towns. Their natural outlet is a rail haul to eastern Canada. In order to sell their lumber export, they must put it in scows, perhaps tow it around from False creek to Vancouver harbour, unload from the scow into the ship which goes overseas. Under the quota system which is now 50 per cent, these domestic mills are being forced into a business for which they were never designed.
A comparison of the figures in relation to the large mills which have timber limits and so on and those in relation to the small mills which have no timber limits, no towing facilities and which are being forced to seek a market in an unnatural sphere will show that a great hardship is being borne by these small mills.
The minister said that if the cost of logs has gone up too much let there be a buyers' strike and the cost will come down. The minister knows as well as I that logs are

quite scarce and that any refusal to buy the logs offered would mean an almost immediate shut-down by the log buying mills. Surely the minister is not suggesting that they should shut down and cease production in order to get the log price down.
The last thing I want to point out with respect to conditions in the lumber trade on the Pacific coast is that the small log buying mill started this year not making a profit on its domestic business. Since that time there has been a $6 increase in the price of logs and a S2 per thousand increase in the cost of labour; that is, the hands in the sawmill itself. They have lost the ten cent premium oij the dollar on their United States business. The domestic quota has been increased from 35 to 50 per cent. At the spring session of the legislature the working week was reduced from forty-eight hours to forty-four hours. No great complaint is being made against any one of these things taken by itself, but when an industry which was not making a profit on its domestic business suffers five such blows wdthin a few weeks it indicates that before the end of the year the earning position of these mills will become seriously impaired. I urge the minister to look into this matter, because I believe in this particular case he will be able to And something to his advantage in his efforts to stimulate the supply of lumber.

My hon. friend has made out a good case for the small mill to present to the wartime prices and trade board for an increase in prices. I do not see why these mills do not present their case. I am assured by the wartime prices and trade board that no case has been made for an increase in prices at this time, and I am also told by that board that when a case can be made an increase will be considered.

I have just one question I should like to ask the minister. I think he said a moment ago that it was the business of the lumber controller to see that the home market was supplied. The hon. member for Vancouver North gave some figures which, if they were correct, would prove that ample lumber is now being produced in Canada to supply the home market and to permit the export provided for. His claim was that it was not being properly distributed, and I wish to know from the minister where the difficulty lies. I should like to know whether the controller is not controlling, or whether the figures given by the hon. member for Vancouver North are incorrect.

Housing Act
I referred to distribution within British Columbia; I quoted no authority for distribution outside the province.
It is British Columbia that I am talking about, because we have a problem in Prince George which is similar to the problem that exists elsewhere. I want to know where the trouble lies.

I do not know of any surpluses of lumber anywhere in Canada. It seems to me that there has been a fair job done in distributing lumber. All the lumber is consumed somewhere. The export quota is certainly being met in full and, so far as I know, all parts of Canada have a reasonable quantity of lumber. For a time we had great difficulty in getting lumber in to southern Saskatchewan. It was much easier to ship across the border. That was worked out, and arrangements have been made which, I think, have brought about a reasonably equitable distribution of lumber so far as geography is concerned. If there are accumulations in one part and shortages in another, that would indicate that the distribution was not reasonably even.

Is the controller limited to geographical considerations, or has he power to distinguish between industries and certain human needs? Can he not give direction to some extent as to which industry shall be supplied with lumber and whether it shall go for homes or for something else?

About thirty per cent of all small homes and a much larger percentage of the homes for veterans, are built under priorities, and special arrangements are made to divert materials into these homes. The remainder of the material goes into the retail market, and no control is exercised over what is built with that lumber.
There has been some discussion about the federal government assuming the over-all programme of construction control. It has been said that it is difficult for a city to do so, because the city may want an industry, and it would be difficult to say no to that industry; regardless of the need of lumber for homes. That bland assumption would indicate that it is very simple for the federal government to exercise similar control. But of all the controls which the federal government attempted to operate in time of war-and I think our wartime controls were more successful than those in any other country-we failed miserably in exercising construction control. Why? Because no one would accept our judgment as to what was essential building 63260-253
and what was not. We received terrific pressures from cities to allow exemptions from the established rules. Black marketing got so bad that the situation became quite uncontrollable. We had more difficulty in getting convictions for black marketing against building control than against any other control. It was practically impossible to obtain a conviction. There would be a flagrant violation of the control in some cities; a prosecution would take place, and the offender would be fined $5 and given a clean bill of health to go ahead. I am willing to operate any control that can be operated, but I know from experience that the federal government cannot successfully operate building control. Just as an example, a delegation of six mayors from large cities came to see me just after we passed the order in council permitting municipalities to operate building control. They said, "We cannot do this because it would never be uniform." They said: "We want you to prohibit certain types of buildings." I said, "I shall be delighted, if you will tell me what types of building to prohibit. Tell me and I will pass the order in council to-morrow." Some said: "Theatres." I said, "Fine; we will start with theatres." Then one mayor spoke up and said, "We have been trying for years to get a theatre built in my city and one is coming along now. You are not going to prohibit theatres." Somebody else said, "Prohibit luxury hotels." At once another mayor spoke up and said, "You are not going to prohibit hotels because we are promoting a hotel to be built in my city and we are going to have it in spite of anything you do." Two or three other types were mentioned, such as bowling alleys. Hon. gentlemen would think that surely we could prohibit bowling alleys during the war, but we had more trouble with bowling alleys being bootlegged than almost anything else. Finally I said to this group of mayors, "Perhaps you will retire and come back later when you have agreed on what you would like prohibited." They met all next day, but they never came back. So I wish that hon. members would drop the idea that the federal government is quite capable of telling people what they can use lumber for and what not.
What about the distribution of lumber? Is it not possible for the timber controller to see that there is an equitable distribution of lumber?

I believe that is being done. I should like to know of inequalities in the distribution of lumber as between geograohical areas.

Housing Act
I mean within a geographical area, is it not possible for there to be an equitable distribution?
I am certain that if the industry within an area could agree on what is an equitable distribution, the timber controller would be glad to see the distribution made accordingly.

I have a further letter from the B. C. Lumber Survey Limited, dated July 26, 1946, in which they say:
What is certain, however,

That is referring to the minister's statement on page 3709 of Hansard:
What is certain, however, is that Mr. Rosen-berry and the wartime prices and trade board were fully informed on the subject and have been so informed for a good many months. Mr. Rosenberry and Mr. Ashbaugh of the wartime prices and trade board received a delegation of the retail lumber men in Vancouver at the beginning of 1946. The only subject discussed at that meeting was the distribution of lumber, the yards having made the request that the board's policy of equitable distribution be applied to lumber. Thus Mr. Howe's department was fully informed that lumber is not being distributed on the 1941 basis and nothing has been done in Vancouver to implement this policy of the board.
Why cannot that policy be implemented in Vancouver?
I shall be glad to call that to the attention of the timber controller.

Nobody has spoken so far from Ontario, which is suffering from a lumber shortage most of all the provinces. I understand that five billion feet is Canada's normal cut of lumber and that that will be the amount produced this year. More than half of that is produced in British Columbia. The government may have made a mistake in allowing, until recently, 65 per cent to be exported. I also understand that the railways have a priority on about 20 per cent of the whole cut. If that is the case, with. 65 per cent exported, now 50 per cent, and 20 per cent of the whole cut going to the railways, there is only 15 per cent left for ordinary construction, so that only a mere trickle comes from the northwest part of British Columbia toward the east. I am very much surprised that members from Saskatchewan and Alberta are raising so much trouble about this matter, because I learn from several sources, which I believe to be reliable, that the prairie provinces have an advantage over Ontario of $3 a thousand in price, although the lumber coming from British Columbia to Ontario must travel very much farther. As a matter of fact, the

lumber does stop in the prairie provinces, where they have no.t much lumber of their own.
I think I mentioned that British Columbia produces more than half the total cut of five billion feet. Let us, for the sake of argument, say that British Columbia produces two and three-quarter billion feet. Ontario, where there is such a large demand for building, and where the timber is now getting farther and farther back, produces one billion feet. A certain amount of that is hard wood and white pine, which does not go into building construction but is used for furniture and other purposes. The minister has just said that one-third is allowed to be exported. So the amount of lumber produced in Ontario that can be used for housing purposes is not large. Then there is Quebec and the maritime provinces which must grow the greater portion of the remaining one and a quarter billion feet that is produced from these other sources. The minister did not say exactly how much of this latter is allowed to be exported. If it is one-third you will see that, when you take into consideration the demand which is made in the maritimes and in Quebec, there is only a mere trickle coming into Ontario, and on that account we suffer more, perhaps, than any other province from lack of lumber.
I have often wished that in the beginning of the housing crisis the government had not been stampeded to the extent they were, because, as I said at the last session when dealing with this question, during the war the government were the largest consumer of lumber and they must have had and did have, throughout Ontario especially, buildings containing seasoned lumber, which could have been taken down and the seasoned materials used for the first six or eight months in the erection of new houses. Some person who should have known told me that the recovery could have been 70 or 80 per cent. This provision would have bridged the period between the time wTe needed lumber for building and such time as new lumber in a more seasoned condition would become more readily available.
I have often wished that the government had erected a more permanent type of building in their housing operations. I have mentioned once or twice before, and many other members have risen in their places in the house and made valid complaints about the situations in which these veterans' houses were built. That is, they were not built in urban districts, although they were meant for urban workers, but were located some distance out. I do not believe that the matter of a half acre of land surrounding a building would

Housing Act
make up for the increased inconvenience the occupier would have in getting to work, or the extra expense involved in putting in different services, such as electricity, water and sewage, as well as the extra trouble the man would have in providing schooling for his family. However, the government did go out some distance, partly necessitated by the fact that they did not provide a more durable type of building. I will mention one municipality I know of, the township of York, which, as some hon. members know, is supposed to be a rural district, although there may be eighty-three thousand people in that comparatively small area, making it the largest rural municipality in Canada. But there are still unoccupied streets, although maybe not paved, provided with sewers, water and electricity, on which houses could have been built if the government had consented to erect them with brick, or concrete blocks, or some other substantial material. Had the government done this there would have been a great saving of lumber. An amount of 15,000 feet has been spoken of to-day as the amount of lumber in a house. I am not a builder or a lumber man, but it strikes me that that is exaggerated for the type of building which has been erected by the government for the veterans. Indeed I would say that half that figure would be more nearly correct. Of course, of this amount, the better part of the lumber is used for the trimming and siding, and it is unfortunate that an attempt was not made to provide more substantial material for the outside, so that this good lumber would have been more available for inside work.
During the war we heard a good deal about plastics and other synthetic materials, and that attempts would be made to create buildings entirely different from anything which had been made before. Strange to relate, the building industry is about where it was forty years ago. Mass production has been applied to practically everything except building, but in that industry they are still back in the old times when they produced very slowly, and with manual labour.	Of course to-day
increased labour costs have had much to do with the increased cost of building.
Houses being so necessary, I was interested in what the minister said about demands from municipalities for other buildings. I have not the figures, and my memory may not be very accurate, but I believe that for the month of April last the amount of construction in Canada was something in this ratio: $18 million for dwellings and about $42 million for industrial buildings, for churches, hotels, theatres and other kinds of buildings. That strikes me as a little out of line when we C3260-253J
hear such moving stories as we have heard here from both hon. members of my own party and hon. members belonging to the C.C.F., possibly also hon. members supporting the Liberal party about the shortage of houses. Surely the government should have sufficient control to see that buildings are provided in a more fair proportion as between homes and other types of construction than they have been. To that extent, I believe, the government has failed in its duty.
There is a black market, and if I were asked where these black markets are located I might not be able to tell you of them. When I suggest, to people who know, that about half the lumber which is distributed in Ontario goes to that market they tell me that the estimate is a little low. The reason for that condition, which has been touched upon by several other speakers, including, I believe, the minister and several hon. members from British Columbia, is that the ceiling is actually so low that the man who manufactures the lumber now eliminates the old retailer; he has to sell direct to the customer in order to get a fair return, because these large prices which he gets from the export trade do not balance the results of the very low ceiling and the extra costs of production. The result is that only a large buyer, shall I say a large consumer buyer, is able to secure this lumber, and the small man who ordinarily went to the retailer to get -a few hundred feet of lumber as he needed it cannot find any now, because-I do not care what anybody says-the small retailers are actually without lumber for the people who want it. People tell me that a certain company, which operates more largely in the prairie provinces than anywhere else, and in a small way in Ontario, is well supplied with lumber. I thought there was something strange about that, and I inquired from a man who has no reason to wish to do the government either a favour or an injury. He said it was because that particular company has always been a large buyer, and its very large buying power enabled it to purchase where the small man could not do so. That does not represent equality of distribution; and I think, since the government has undertaken this job, it might do it a little more equitably.

Would the minister explain a statement of his on the resolution stage with regard to the assistance being given to manufacturers of building materials to get increased production? Would he give the committee an idea of the type of obstacles they are encountering, the methods he is using to meet them, and what is being done about increasing the capacity of various lines in the country?
Housing Act
I shall be very glad to do so. Would my hon. friend like me to do so now?
I think this is the proper time. As far as I know, there is no part of the bill which deals with it.
It is almost six o'clock. Would it be all right to do it at eight o'clock?

There is a distribution as between areas. Would the minister tell us whether that applies also to such supplies as steel? Since the discussion on July 22 I have had a letter from Smith Sheet Metal Works Ltd., Vancouver. They state:
We are, and have been for thirty years, the only manufacturer of metal cornerbead, west of Winnipeg We are not able to obtain sheets for the production of cornerbead this year, although we have approached the steel controller on several occasions for a quota for this purpose.
Under normal circumstances, we acquire our requirements from the Canadian steel mills through a local supplier.
Due to the shortages, however, they will no longer accept an order for this purpose as it would come off their small monthly quota. As a result, we are not able to supply^ metal head, and the housing programme is being seriously held up. The eastern manufacturers are able to get sheets for this purpose and ship the goods out here.
I presume, the manufactured goods.
We feel that this is certainly very discriminating inasmuch as we are an old-time manufacturer of this article. Last year we produced three-quarters of a million feet, whereas this year to date we have turned out only 20,000 feet. We have tried to obtain from the steel controller, a definite quota per month but as yet we have received nothing but a run around, as he refers us to our local suppliers who in turn refer us to the steel controller.
What should a person do in a case like that?

The administrator of the wartime prices and trade board has that matter in charge. My over-all experience is that supplies of sheet metal on the Pacific coast have been better than in the east for the last several months. Evidently this man has depended on a supplier who has let him down. Ordinarily each industry has its own supplier and it is the duty of the administrator of the wartime prices and trade board to see that suppliers get their fair share of the over-all production. I think my hon. friend1 will find that this man's usual supplier gets his fair share.
Is there anyone to compel the local supplier to supply him with the material?

If he can make a good case, the administrator will no doubt try to see that he is kept in business.
{Mr. Merritt.]

Will there be restricted areas in the application- of the act? Will there be any parts of Canada where loans will not be made available? There was a time under the National Housing Act when we could not get anything in Swift Current. Shall we be able to get any now?

Yes. The whole effort over the last several months has been to make sure that every part of Canada will obtain service. That is the purpose of the amendment. It is to make sure that rural areas and areas producing raw products will get the same service as is obtained in t.he cities.

Will the minister give
the committee figures for various parts of Canada, including Vancouver, as to the estimated cost of constructing per square foot of, say a house under S6,000, and the lending value per square foot-whatever figure is used by the National Housing Act authorities?

We have never released these prices. It is difficult to say. Under integrated housing there is a controlled price which would be a criterion. The floor price for speculative building would be something else. We can hardly give it.

I am only asking with respect to the estimated cost upon which the lending value of the loan to the home owner is based. Since the lending value must be established, and he must be told what that is, there should not be any secrecy about that particular cost.

The variation in lending value depends on the location of the house, the desirability, and various other factors. If we laid down a rigid lending value for any kind of house in any location, such procedure would be hardly fair to the lending authorities. The only way in which the prospective buyer can get a lending value on a house is to produce the plans and location of the house. Then he is given the lending value of that particular house.

In my speech this morning I quoted the figures $4.20 and $6 which I got out of a report in a Vancouver newspaper respecting certain houses there. The minister has placed his limit of ten per cent on the increase in the lending value squarely on the ground that the cost of building houses has gone up 150 per cent from 1939, and, as I said, if that is so his argument in his statement the other day is one with which I agree. But when I see a spread of SI.80 per square foot between the lending value and the actual cost in connection with a particular house in

Housing Act
Vancouver, then I am led to believe that the actual cost must have gone up very much more than 150 per cent since 1939. Therefore, the actual increase of ten per cent in lending value, so far as I can see, is not going to relieve at all the situation which it was designed to relieve.

It is necessary to see the plan of the house before we can say whether the figures given by my hon. friend are valid, as regards the difference he mentions. If it is a controlled-cost plan of building, the spread is entirely out of proportion. If costs are controlled the spread should be very much less than that mentioned. In the case of the speculative builder, the purchaser makes his own deal, but I would be surprised if he went ahead on the basis of the spread indicated. I know of no way in which the government can protect that man against an exorbitant profit of the builder.
