After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 2-"Cost of construction".

Before the recess, I undertook to answer a question asked by the hon. member for Cariboo, I believe, as to what methods were used for stimulating production. In my remarks on the resolution, I stated that we were prepared to use the same methods for stimulating production of home building materials that were used for stimulating the production of war materials during the war period. Various methods have been used to increase the production of nails. We examined the industry and found that a price increase was required, and a price increase was granted. In the case of asbestos, an amount representing a very large investment was made by a private company in return for receiving double the usual rate of depreciation. In the matter of plumbing supplies, negotiations are now proceeding which may involve the government paying for certain equipment, under the proviso that the government will own the equipment until the cost of it has been refunded through depreciation account or otherwise. In the case of brick, new brickyards were opened by government assistance in providing labour; and also in one case by the government undertaking to purchase the output of the yard in the event that the brick could not be sold privately. In the case of wallboard, an old mill was opened by the government diverting raw material from the industry as a whole and undertaking to purchase any material that could not be sold privately at the ceiling price.
These are samples of devices that have been used in stimulating production. A great number of cases have been examined and have received treatment. In the matter of soil pipe, it was felt the difficulty was that the ceiling was too low, and the ceiling was adjusted in a manner that greatly increased production. The practice is to examine a situation, find out what is preventing the required expansion, and then to take remedial steps accordingly.

Has the minister considered adding another safeguard which, in my opinion, is exceedingly necessary. I believe that the production of all these items the minister has mentioned can vary considerably within the plants themselves. That is, production may be either slowed down or speeded up by a variety of more or less artificial devices: at the wish of the management, for example; continuous delay in getting a spare part, and so on. Has the minister considered making part and parcel of any contract he has entered into with any of these various industrial groups a requirement that double shifts, or three shifts if necessary, be maintained in the plants? What is the safeguard with respect:, to seeing that this machinery is continuously* employed? That is extremely important. Certainly it is a rnuph more difficult thing for the minister to assure than it would be to say, "We shall raise the price of nails from $5 to $6.50."

In examining a situation the first question asked is, is the industry operating at full capacity; in other words, is it operating three shifts? If not, the first step taken is to bring it into three shift operation and to correct any difficulties that prevented that being done previously. It is very simple for the officer in charge to check whether a plant continues to operate with three shifts, because the rate of production on a three-shift basis is established and any drop in production calls for an explanation.

Is it possible for any company manufacturing bathtubs or boilers or iron pipe fittings or soil pipe to get enough pig-iron to operate to capacity on one shift,
Housing Act

let alone three shifts? Is not the trouble with all such businesses to-day the question of pig-iron?

If my hon. friend is talking about to-day, he is quite correct. Before the steel strike, however, the steel controller was supplying industry generally with all the pig-iron it could use. At Algoma Steel we cut back the production of steel by 25 per cent in order that the coke and other supplies required for making cast-iron could be devoted to that purpose. As long'as the industry was working at capacity under government direction, I do not think anyone requiring pig-iron failed to get the amount needed.

That is, of course, the real problem. Before the strike, we were forcing our steel economy to the limit. But up to that time, while everyone using pig-iron was on the ragged edge, I know of no case where an industry had to shut down for any considerable length of time owing to a lack of pig-iron. We were just about getting by with what makeshifts we could use. No industry had any considerable stock of pig-iron, but all were getting current supplies sufficient for immediate needs, so far as I know.
In the matter of nails, we have been running our industry to capacity. The present curtailment in production of nails is due to the curtailment in production of steel rods, as well as strikes in one or two of the nail plants. Of course we have plenty of steel rods inside a picket line at one plant, but unfortunately they are not available at the present time. The industry is completely disorganized to-day, and it will be a matter of several weeks before we get back into our stride. But when we do, I think we shall be reasonably in balance, so far as raw materials of steel are concerned.

Will the minister assure the committee that the capacity of the building materials industry in the country is great enough to deal with the programme of housing he envisages for the next five years? Will he say at the same time whether that capacity is such that the programme could be increased over the figures he has given?

The reason the limit to the programme is set is to keep parallel with our ability to expand the materials market. The reason we set 60,000 houses for the current year is that we believed we could raise our sights on the required materials in order to produce 60,000 houses. The reason we have set 80,000 for next year is that we believe we can raise our sights on materials to supply 80,000 houses. The following year we believe we can hit the 100,000 level, and keep up our supply of materials.
But the supply of materials is the wholly governing factor in the number of houses. If we had twice as much material, and a sufficient amount of labour, we could build twice as many houses this year. We are forcing up this materials position as rapidly as we can, and as rapidly as experience tells us is possible of attainment. That is the wholly limiting factor in the number of houses to be built.

I should like to ask a question respecting devices which the minister indicated were used to increase production of materials necessary for the building of houses. Is it not so that to offer increases in prices

Housing Act
to private corporations to increase certain products means that pressure is brought to bear upon price ceiling control? In the second place, does the minister not think it is a weak device to remove from any private corporation all risk whatsoever, and promise to take over any surplus which may be left after the building programme begins to slacken? In that event, the community is absorbing the entire loss; or, if the surplus materials are put on the market subsequently, it means that the companies will have to shorten their production, just as if the device had never been put there.

The agreements are made for a limited period, perhaps for two or three years. We are in the happy position that we are most anxious to step up our programme, and to use any surplus materials. We feel we are quite safe in guaranteeing to take the entire output, because we are delighted to step up our programme so that we can be sure of the housing output. In other words, we have an expanding demand, and any temporary surplus of materials, which has almost never occurred and is not likely to occur, would be bought by us and put aside until we could step up the over-all production to a place which would allow us to reabsorb that material.

What are the prospects for securing galvanized iron? In my part of the country I know of a number of buildings now under construction, but the people who are supplying the heating equipment in considerable quantities are short of galvanized iron.
At the present time the prospects are just terrible. Not a pound is being made in Canada.
I was afraid of that.

I should like to ask
another question, to which I would expect the same answer. When I was home over the week-end I discussed the question of glass with a large dispenser of that product. I gathered from him that there will not be a pound of glass anywhere in their organization for some time.
Time is rapidly going on. Here we are almost to the first of August. A month from that, people will be protecting themselves against inclement weather. What can they do? Are any big buildings available to be refitted to accommodate the multitudes of people who are living in tents? It is not the industry's fault. Everything is being held up at the present time and the situation may
get worse. It is not the minister's fault or mine. But we must look forward to saving our people from freezing to death, or suffering bad health from exposure to weather. The next month will go by rapidly, and when that time is over we are up against it.

I am happy to say the situation respecting window glass is not as bad as that in connection with steel. It is true that our glass-making industry is gradually closing down, owing to a strike in a plant which manufactures soda ash.
But window glass is not made on a large scale in Canada. I made the mistake of saying in an earlier debate that it was not made here at all. It was called to my attention that we have one plant, Industrial Glass Works Limited, St. Laurent, Quebec, which manufactures glass, and which is back in business.
However, imports of window glass are improving. Belgium, which was one of our great pre-war sources of window glass, is gradually coming back into the market, and in the meantime imports from the United Kingdom and the United States are stepping up slowly, as well. So that I think in the matter of window glass we are fairly well off.

Has the minister taken the precaution of leaving an avenue open for the renegotiation of prices he is currently allowing producers, in case the profit margin gets too high, in the opinion of the government; or has the minister left that to look after itself?

Contracts made to-day are not subject to renegotiation. But the position of the manufacturer is closely examined before increases are granted. I believe that adequate precaution is being taken to make sure that excessive price increases are not granted.

I learned only a few days ago from a soldier who had served overseas for five years some facts concerning the purchase of a house. When he came back he had to find a house for his bride and his child, and went to the organization set up for that purpose. Its name escapes my memory at the moment. He bought the house from them at $6,000. Upon going back later to inquire as to when he could get possession, he was told that it would now cost $6,500, and after he waited for some time longer and made a further inquiry, the price of the house had gone up to $7,000. I was just wondering what controls there were in connection with Wartime Housing.

Wartime Housing does not sell houses. I am sure my hon. friend is referring to the Veterans Land Act. I am not familiar with its operations.
Homing Act

Mr. MaoNICOL: Does it get its supplies from the government?
That comes under the Department of Veterans Affairs.

When I spoke a moment ago I said that I was not familiar with the name and I referred to it as Wartime Housing. However, after hearing what the minister has said I realize that it is the Veterans Land Act. Is there any authority to prevent them from advancing the price of a house after making a contract with a returned soldier? I do not believe any working man or any ordinary chap would be able in his lifetime to pay for a house costing $7,500, unless he had perfect health and had no trouble in his home or was not faced with many of the problems that confront people in his circumstances. God must love these people more than he loves the others because he makes so many of them. Their troubles are legion. I do not believe any ordinary man, even in a reasonable length of time, would be able to pay for a $7,500 house.

I should like to be assured by the minister that I shall have an opportunity to return to the matter of cooperative housing schemes which, so far, have not been able to use the provisions of the act. I believe this matter would come under section 9 of the old act, and I should like to ask the minister if it will be appropriate for me to discuss this matter under section 5 of the present bill?
My hon. friend spoke of United States legislation, but I think he has become confused between bills introduced in congress and legislation. Was it the Wagner bill he was discussing?
It is No. S-1592, sections 404 and 405.
That is the so-called Wagner-Ellender-Taft bill. It has been introduced in the senate, and it is having a rather rough time there if one can believe the press.
It is still living.

It is like the amendments to the National Housing Act; it is under consideration. That bill refers to a project constructed by a non-profit corporation organized for the purpose of the construction of homes for members of the corporation. That provision is in the proposed amendment, but it is not in the present legislation. The present national housing act of the United States reads as follows:
Loans under section 207 of this title are rental housing loans made to limited-dividend corporations.

Those are corporations offering housing for rent but not for ownership.
A loan may not exceed $5,000,000 in amount, nor more than 80 per cent of the administrator's estimated valuation of the completed property, nor more than $1,350 per room attributable to dwelling use. (In no case can loan exceed 100 per cent of administrator's estimate of building cost.) Amortization basis is stipulated in each case by the administrator.
That applies to a limited-dividend corporation erecting housing for rent. There is no provision in the present United States legislation, as I read it, for cooperative building of homes to be owned by the members.
That is a good reason why we should take the first step. I ask the minister if it will be appropriate for me to bring up the matter under section 5?
Quite.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-"Economic rental of a family housing unit."

This section provides that the economic rental means an annual rental at the rate of twelve per cent of the cost of construction of the family housing unit. That is the basis for the working out of the rent chargeable by a corporation when arriving at its contract with its tenant. Could the minister give us the background for this twelve per cent rate? I have no doubt it is -based on good business practice, but I would presume that if we were able to get money at one or two per cent, or something like that, we might be able to reduce that annual -rent to considerably less than twelve per cent.

This is on the basis of one per cent per month. That may not be a very good explanation. I am not very familiar with the act since I was not in on the drafting. This amendment makes no change in the original act in that regard. I cannot tell my hon. friend why one per cent per month is considered to be an economic rental, but apparently the present act provides for that.

It must be based on some financial consideration, and no doubt all the factors that entered into the cost of the house are considered, plus the maintenance, interest on the principal, depreciation, taxes and the replenishment of capital after thirty or forty years. The National Housing Act permits that a housing corporation set up by an insurance company may charge an economic rent of twelve per cent of the cost of the housing project and still be eligible for a government guarantee in the event of loss.

One per cent per month is the maximum that can be charged and it is

Housing Act
adjusted down if the facts do not justify that economic rental. In other words, if all the items mentioned by my hon. friend add up to less than one per cent per month, the economic rental is limited accordingly.

The National Housing Act of last year and the amendments of this year refer to the twelve per cent. That would make the rental of a $5,000 house total $500 a year, while the rent of a $3,000 house would be $300 a year. If we are interested in low-rental housing it seems to me that we must work out some basis where we do not have an economic rental of around twelve per cent of the cost of the house.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-"Housing project".

This new section will read:
"housing project" means a project consisting of one or more one-family dwellings, or one or more multiple-family dwellings, or a combination of one-familv and multiple-family dwellings, together with any public space, recreational facilities and commercial space and buildings appropriate to the project.
Later clauses of the National Housing Act refer to such things as community planning. There have been put up in my city several hundred structures for which we thank Wartime Housing Limited and other agencies, because they keep the weather off the inmates of those houses, but when I think of the beautiful little city we had before these structures were put up and what we have now from the point of view of community or city planning I consider it nothing less than a disgrace. I think the minister should consider adding these words to the end of this section, "consistent with recognized planning principles." Would the minister comment on that?

Section 9 I think covers the point my hon. friend mentions. It protects the standards and provides for suitable community planning. If my hon. friend is talking to me as a former resident of Regina about wartime housing spoiling the character of the city, surely that is a matter for debate.
We had a planning commission in our city for twenty years, and they have been trying to remove some of the scars left by our earlier pioneers.
Be careful.

Including my good friend the hon. member for Calgary West, who was at one time a resident of our city. When we are discussing planning principles I think we should be consistent in our definitions. That is the only reason I bring this matter to the
minister's attention. There is nothing here to indicate that we have in mind the planning of our cities.
That comes later.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-"Limited-dividend housing company."

I want to bring to the attention of the minister once again the plea of cooperative organizations to come under section 9 of the National Housing Act. I have here the prospectus of the York Mills Cooperative Home Builders' Association, which was granted a charter by the province of Ontario on December 3, 1945. The prospectus sets forth the objectives of the association, conditions of membership, methods of financing, building, tenancy and ownership. This newly organized cooperative, having been granted letters patent, made their application to the proper authorities to be granted a loan on a basis similar to that for private corporations for the purpose of building houses to be rented at a low rental to the shareholders of the association until such time as thirty years had elapsed, by which time the house would become the property of those who had lived in it and had paid back the loan. They received a reply from the department stating, in effect, that no provision was made for making loans for the building of homes that would be ultimately owned by those who rented them, and consequently the whole project has been brought to a standstill.
Would the minister give the committee a real reason why a cooperative should be excluded from section 9 of the housing act? It seems to me to be an act which provides for the c-are particularly of insurance and loan companies. According to the act, on a house costing $7,000 to build, 95 per cent of the first $2,000, or $1,900, may be borrowed; 85 per cent of the second $2,000, or $1,700; 70 per cent of the next $3,000. or $2,100; making a total to be borrowed' under the terms of the act of $5,700 out of the $7,000. It appears that under this section of the act private corporations scheme so that, by borrowing the full amount which the act provides for, they can increase the payments of the borrower by a considerable amount, so that instead of an actual loan of $5,700 on a house of $7,000 they manage to get away with lending $4,410. Thus, instead of 81 per cent of the loan, they are granting 47 per cent of the loan. So it would appear that the act as it is working out is one which, chiefly benefits the lending institutions.
The point I wish to make is this. In the first place, is not the security of the property
Housing Act

in question, supported by a cooperative organization, just as good collateral, if you like, or just as good a guarantee of repayment of the loan as that given by a limited liability company, or whatever name may be given to the corporation which will borrow the money and build these houses? In the last analysis, the only real security you have is the house itself. If a man fails to meet his payments under this cooperative plan the property will, of course, be taken over by those who made the loan, just as it would in the case of a private corporations making the loan.
In the second place, why should the government insist that houses should always be rented? When a man has been in a house for thirty years and has paid the full amount of the money borrowed, why should he continue to rent it? Should it not be his house? That is the proposal Which the cooperative makes. I want the minister to give that serious consideration. I should like the minister to satisfy the committee-and I hope I am not the only one who is not satisfied with things as they are now-that it is not right or that it is not practicable or fair or whatever he wants to say about it, to make provision for a cooperative to borrow under this scheme. If he cannot explain that satisfactorily, I trust that he will make a new provision in the bill to permit the cooperative to obtain a loan which is now available only to private corporations which insist that homes in Canada shall always be rented and never be owned by the people themselves.

I should like to read a letter that I have received from a group organized in British Columbia along the lines my hon. friend has just mentioned, together with a short brief which they have presented, and this is only one group Which is considering making similar proposals. This letter is from a group of veterans in the university of British Columbia who have organized to form a Veterans' Cooperative Building Association. It reads:
Dear sir:
I enclose for your consideration a copy of a brief prepared by the Veterans' Cooperative Building Association, of which I have the honour to be president.
Our association was originally legion sponsored, but is now quite independent, although all members are veterans.
We have had every encouragement in our plans from all sources, including the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and now have our building plans complete for an initial project of 52 units.	-
I feel sure you appreciate the housing emergency in Vancouver, and will give the enclosed material your earnest consideration and support.
Yours truly,
D. Brousson,
President.
They deal with the subject in this short brief:
This brief is prepared and presented by the Veterans' Cooperative Building Association, 553 Granville St., Vancouver, B.C.
This association was formed last fall under the sponsorship of branch 168 of the Canadian Legion in Vancouver, in an attempt to help veterans solve their own housing problems, by providing moderate rental accommodation on a mutual ownership basis.
With this in view, the association has applied for a loan from the Central Mortgage and Housing Act, 1944, to finance an initial project. Loans under this section bear interest at 3 per cent, repayable within fifty years.
In doing so, the association has agreed _ to submit to all the requirements of the section as regards limitation of dividends, rents and incomes in order to insure the low-rental character of the project.
The central mortgage and housing committee, *while approving the technical details of the project, has refused the loan on the ground that because we are a cooperative association this would not be a rental housing project, but in essence a form of home ownership, and therefore disqualified under the term of section 9.
This association does not consider this decision to be soundly based from a legal point of view since the identity of a body corporate and of its membership are separate and distinct things and while it is true the tenants would hold shares in the association, tenants might also hold shares in a joint stock company and at the same time rent houses from it. but this would not presumably disqualify -such -a corporation from operating under this section of the act. In other words, the decision appears to discriminate directly against the cooperative type of organization.
I am not. going to read the rest of the brief, and take the time of the committee in so doing. However, in addition to the questions placed before the minister by the hon. member for Cariboo, I should like the minister to explain why he considers that this is not a practical scheme, a scheme such as has been in successful operation in Great Britain, I believe, for at least fifty years, where the money had to be raised from outside capital. The loans were subscribed in the form of bonds or debentures to form a building association. These associations in Great Britain have had a successful history; you rarely hear of a failure; they have been successful in every way, and I should like the minister to explain why he does not consider, under our present conditions, the necessities of the times and the urge of these men to cooperate in doing something for themselves, that something of that type would not be practicable and satisfactory in this country.

My hon. friend suggests as a parallel an organization which has been successful in England. I suggest that that is not the case. The cooperative building societies in England are corporations of substance; they build houses for rent and they also build

Housing Act
houses for sale. I gave the parallel before dinner; I do not know that I need repeat it. We will say the number will be ten-ten men banding together to form a cooperative. For what purpose? To build houses for themselves to own. That is the real purpose of the thing. The trouble is that the cooperative has no substance. Each man puts in what he expects his own house to cost, no more. If one of the tenants gets into difficulty a flaw is thrown on the title of the entire project, or might be. There is no substance to fall back on if one of the tenants gets into any of the ordinary business difficulties which might be experienced by any one of the cooperators. Therefore it is not a corporation that is desirable from the point of view of the cooperators, and it is not a type of business which is desirable for a government lending institution or any other lending institution. There is no reason why ten people should gather together for this purpose. Under part I of the Housing Act each can build his own house and be better off, because he has title to the property at all stages and has everything under his own control. We believe that it is not good business for the government to support a type of organization that is not businesslike as far as its own internal arrangements are concerned and offers to the government no protection which it would not have in dealing with the members individually.

I still have to press the point that the minister has not shown that there is not quite as good security under the cooperative arrangement as under any other, for the only guarantee that the government will have from any of these private corporations will be the building itself, and that will still be there. If it burns down it will have been insured. The minister says that there will be the same advantage for a private individual to do it himself. Let me show the minister that he is quite wrong in that. This is from the estimate of a company newly formed, of which I spoke, the Cooperative Association of Home Builders, in Toronto. Here is what they propose. On a house costing $6,000 the rental charge at prevailing rates would be $40 a month. Principal and interest charges on $5,400 amortized over thirty years at three per cent would 'be $22.84; interest on membership equity, one per cent on $590 corporate equity, would be fifty cents; municipal taxes, approximately $6; vacancy allowance, $1; insurance, sixty cents; special sinking fund for retiring thirty year loan made by each of the applicants, $1.23; making a total carrying charge per month of $32.17. So that there would be paid back each month to the cooperators $7.83, which would go to private corporations under the scheme which is provided for in the act, and would be $7.83 a month more for the wage-earners to pay in order to get their homes. So that it does make a difference whether it is done cooperatively or done under a private corporation.

There is a further point, arising from the brief submitted by the organization referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay West, this veterans' organization in Vancouver. As they point out, if they are ruled out from the operation of section 9 of the act, then as a cooperative they would have to operate under section 4, where the rate of interest on loans is 4i per cent per annum, instead of three per cent, which it is under section 9. The point the organization makes seems to me to be a good one and not to have been answered by the minister; that is to say, that just because they are a cooperative organization instead of a limited company does not mean that they cannot as a cooperative enter into a project for the construction of homes which they will rent to their members.
Quite so. Will they keep to that business, though? If they do that they can qualify under this part.
I do not know whether they will or not.
If they stop right there they qualify.
They have been ruled out apparently on the ground-
They won't keep to that.

It seems to be a fine distinction which the minister is drawing. If they will form a cooperative for the purpose of entering this arrangement with the institution and renting to members it would be all right, but what is the objection when they start to allow members to buy from a cooperative? Where does the risk become a bad one?
They are getting into a different class of business.
They may be getting into a different class of business, but what is the change in the risk? Why is it less desirable from the government's point of view?

Well, I put the thing on Hansard yesterday. I would be glad to put it on to-day:
Under part I of the act joint loans are available to cooperative housing groups formed for the purpose of building houses or apartments for occupancy by members of the group. Under certain circumstances loans for rental housing projects may also be made under part II . . .

Housing Act
At 4J per cent.

Yes, that is right, provided that the corporation is already formed and has interests other than housing.
Applications are being received from coopera'-tive groups for loans at three per cent for periods up to fifty years under section 9 of the act. This section provides for loans to limited-dividend companies for low rental housing projects,
Mark the distinction-low rental housing projects.
Generally these applications are from groups of individuals being formed into a cooperative to build houses for their own occupancy with the equity being supplied by themselves. The form of arrangement involves a lease to the member of the cooperative, but in most respects the position of the member is that of a home owner. These applications have been declined because section 9 was not designed for this purpose, its conditions cannot be fulfilled under such circumstances, it was never intended that the tenants of a low-rental limited dividend project should be its owners and the position of the tenant with respect to both his equity and continued occupancy is unsatisfactory.
An individual going into such an arrangement nas no security of tenure because under the terms of section 9 he cannot continue to lease a unit in the low-rental project if his income exceeds five times his rental. This condition exists to assure the low-rental character of the project. Even if the tenant's rental-being paid in lieu of principal, interest and taxes-is current, he has no protection against foreclosure with loss of equity and tenancy if the project as a whole goes into default which might be occasioned by default of 5 per cent or 10 per cent of the tenants. In most of the applications we have received there is no indication of any reasonable measure of protection on this score. Nor are there funds, other than the tenants' equity, to assure completion of the project in a period of rising costs.
The position of the tenant when the loan on the project is repaid is not happy. Under the section he, as part owner of a limited-dividend company, or having an interest in it through a cooperatitve, may not receive more than his equity with 5 per cent interest. If the residual value of his house was greater than this amount he would have to make a corresponding payment to retain possession. If it was decided to sell the property as a whole the position would be even more difficult. To avoid this trouble it has been suggested that at this time we should provide that the units revert to the tenants at the end of the amortization period. This is not possible in the light of the intent of the act.
There are other reasons why we should not approve such applications. They, like the ones I have outlined, all add up to one conclusion. Section 9 was not designed for home owners. Nor was section 9, with long-term money at three per cent, designed as a substitute for part I of the act, which provides loans to home owners at 4J per cent for a term generally twenty years but under some circumstances up to thirty years. If we provide cooperative home-owners with three per cent money, our position becomes difficult with other homeowners.

Our position is very clear. We will not approve applications for loans under section 9 of limited-dividend companies where the prospective tenants directly or indirectly are financing the equity of the project nor where factors exist which are not compatible to a limited-dividend rental project as defined by the act. On the other hand, we are ready to approve such applications under appropriate sections of the act, such as section 4 (3), which makes provision for loans to persons incorporated for the purpose of constructing and managing a cooperative housing project.

A good deal of what the minister has read, it is difficult to digest at once; but listening to it, it struck me that the objections made were equally applicable against a low-dividend corporation, particularly the difficulty which might be encountered should it be desired to buy a whole project- the same difficulty would be encountered with a limited-dividend corporation. That was the main impression I got, that all the difficulties which the minister detailed in that statement were equally applicable to the other form of corporation. I do not see why the risk should be affected merely because the members of the cooperative are given the opportunity, by paying a sum in addition to their rent, to buy the homes so that at the end of the fifty-year period they might own their own homes. It works in this way, surely. If the cooperative puts up the necessary money and can enter into this project with the government and the lending institution, then the cooperative as a body would be bound to pay a certain sum a year to the lending institution. That amount would have to be paid monthly by the members of the cooperative as rent. Provided that they complied with these terms and, in addition, were willing and able to pay the sum, whatever it might be, say ten dollars a month extra, so that at the same time they might be buying their equity in their homes, in what way would the risk to the government be increased? Finally, although the experts in the minister's department may have advised him before this ruling was made, there is nothing in paragraph 24 of section 2 of the act, in the definition of limited-dividend corporation, which in itself excludes a cooperative from the provisions of this section.
It is not the intention to exclude cooperatives. We welcome cooperatives in that field, provided that they carry out the purpose of the section, which is to build low-rental housing.
I know that,

I know you do not understand it, but I am telling you what the purpose of the section is.

Housing Act

And I am asking the
minister whether he can justify such a ridiculous purpose, because if you can build low-rental houses and there is no greater risk in enabling people to buy the houses back, all houses should be put under that section. However, if the minister has made up his mind I will not argue further about the matter, though I do not see the basis of the decision.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does it not boil down to this, that the minister and the government do not wish to make it possible for home owners to get money at three per cent?
Not at all.
That is the effect of it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is precisely the
effect of the ruling that home owners must came under the section that requires payment of four and one-half per cent. This special provision of three per cent is made available only to these other limited-dividend companies or cooperatives who are building homes for rent. The point which we are trying to get across to the minister, and which we tried to get across to the Minister of Finance in the budget debate,, is that this is what cooperatives are for, not to make a profit but to save riioney to the members of the organization. The hon. member for Cariboo has given figures to indicate the type of saving that could be effected. The minister has already admitted that ten individuals in a cooperative in the case he cited could each come under part I of the housing act, and there is certainly no greater risk if the ten of them come together under this proposal. As a matter of fact, there would be less risk because of the nature of cooperatives. It seems to me that what we have here as in the other debate is a failure on the part of the government to recognize the true purpose of cooperatives and their valuable place in our economy.
We shall see how profitable the other branches of the business are.

The minister referred to the fact that the limited-dividend housing companies were intended merely to manage low-rental housing projects. In his definition of a low-rental housing project in section 25 he states an anomalous position, because he refers to a housing project undertaken to provide decent, safe and sanitary housing accommodation to be leased to families of low income, or to such other persons as the corporation, under agreement with the owner, may designate. In other words, I believe it is recognized, and was stated here in the house by one responsible minister of the crown, that these limited-dividend housing corporations were not necessarily entering the low-rental housing field. I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I do not think he can under the circumstances, because it is not intended that the low-rental housing project will be held exclusively for the marginal income group of individuals.
While I am on my feet, I should like to draw attention to the wording of paragraph 25, which is contained in section 5 of this bill. It seems to me, with my limited ability to phrase readable English, that the minister has left a loophole for limited-dividend housing corporations or companies to build slum-type dwellings, if I correctly read the word "exceeding" in line 40. It provides:
"low-rental housing project" means a housing project undertaken to provide decent, safe and
Housing Act

sanitary housing accommodation complying with standards not exceeding those approved by the corporation . . .
Apparently the corporation has certain other housing projects, but a low-rental housing project must not exceed that standard. In other words, it may fall below the standard. I should like the minister to consider rewording this section. My mind is not that of an attorney, as I have said, but to me this is an invitation to a limited-dividend housing company to get into submarginal construction. Perhaps we might have an explanation on that, and at the same time the minister might tell us the reason for the statement that as other, alternative tenants you may have such other persons as the corporation, under agreement with the owner, may designate.

The purpose of the "not exceeding" is, "not exceeding a certain rental." In other words, the government is not prepared to lend three per cent money to build rich men's houses. The purpose is to keep housing financed by the three per cent loans down to reasonable rental. I may say that Housing Enterprises Limited is very much a borderline case. It is not the type of rental we hope to get with those loans. The standards of construction are, of course, approved by the corporation. The plans and specifications are submitted to the corporation and approved by it as well as by the local building authorities before any agreement is entered into. The "not exceeding" applies wholly to the economic rental.

I applaud that meaning and intent on the part of the minister; but just listen to this again:
... a housing project undertaken to provide decent, safe and sanitary housing accommodation complying with standards-
Not rentals, but standards.

not exceeding those approved by the corporation . . .
I defy any person who understands the king's English, or for that matter any lawyer, to tie that up with rentals. I think the minister must re-word this section.
Section agreed to:
On section 6-Powers of approved lending institution to loan on first mortgage.

I have an amendment to this section which I would ask my colleague the Minister of Justice to move.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I move:
That section 3 of the act as reenacted by section 6 of the bill be amended by adding immediately after the last word thereof the following:

"and to protect the mortgage security, the said lending institution and the corporation may join in makim- supplementary joint loans to the borrower and in the taking of such other measures and steps as may be required in accordance with normal mortgage practice, to safeguard the interests of His Majesty and the said lending institution."
Might we have an. explanation of that?

The purpose of the amendment is to assure that the lending institution and the corporation have power to perform the normal functions of a mortgagee in the handling of a joint mortgage account. It is occasionally necessary in the handling of a mortgage account to advance money for taxes, insurance premiums and other matters affecting the security, and in some cases to advance money to take foreclosure action. These are specific examples of what might be done under this clause. I may say the auditor general has expressed doubt as to whether the act permits the mortgage company to make expenditures of the type I have mentioned, to protect the property. In the case of a farm, it might be necessary to advance money as a loan for seed grain; and in a city it is frequently necessary to advance money to pay taxes to prevent loss of the property to the city. This is simply to make it abundantly clear that the corporation has the right to advance money for those purposes.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 7-Contract with approved lending institution in respect to loans and resulting losses for rural housing.

This section deals with the approval or at least with the inspection of farm homes for the purpose of lending money to be used in erecting houses on such farms. As was mentioned by several speakers this afternoon, to date the farm loan clause has been a failure. According to a recent report to the house, there was supposed to be one loan for farm housing alive somewhere in Canada. I paid a visit to the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation a short time ago, in part to find out where this house was, but apparently he was in some doubt as to whether there was even that one loan in existence. There must be some reason why farmers have not been able to avail themselves of the terms of the National Housing Act. Would the minister indicate how extensively farmers have applied for assistance under this act, and what their reception has been. The absence of any loans in Canada in

Housing Act
ten or eleven years suggests to me that the act is not meeting with very favourable response, and that there must be a reason for it.

There have been no applications for loans under the farm section. The one loan referred to was in Davidson, Saskatchewan, which I would describe as an urban rather than a farm loan. That application was made under this section. The reason is that, administratively, the section has proved to be impossible.
Are you now amending it?

We are amending it to make it workable, we think; and we hope to have it widely used as amended. The terms are being liberalized, and provision is being made for handling costs in connection with the making of loans, which are very much higher than costs in urban centres.

In view of the fact that the minister's officials are now sitting in front of him, may I point out that under the old National Housing Act there were certain districts where applications for loans were made to lending institutions. Sometimes those lending institutions took the position that, owing to the fact that a city or municipality from which an application came was under heavy bonded indebtedness, objection should be raised to making such loans. I hope that under the new act this will not take place. I call the minister's attention to this point because it acted to the detriment of a person with whom I am acquainted.

Would the minister indicate if the changes he is proposing with respect to farm lending are such that farmers of all provinces, without discrimination, will be able to avail themselves of the terms- of the National Housing Act? I am chiefly interested in Saskatchewan, naturally, where the Central Mortgage and' Housing Corporation has done very little business. I believe that only 199 houses have been built in the last year and a half with money lent by that corporation. Is there to be any discrimination in the matter of lending money for rural homes in Saskatchewan?

The difficulty in making loans
in Saskatchewan arises from provincial legislation. I believe that legislation is being tested before the supreme court, and about the end of October we should know what the position is. Obviously the provincial legislation is in conflict with the requirements of the housing act as it stands on the statute books.

Have there been any negotiations between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Saskatchewan government dealing with those specific points of legislation, in so far as the National Housing Act is concerned?

No, there have been no discussions. I happen to know that the point has been raised by the dominion, on account of the farm loan boards. I understand that a decision will be brought down in two or three months.
There is no question as to the personal responsibility of individuals in that province.
Not at all.
It is just on account of the legislation?
Yes.

Because, after all. some question was raised as to the value of our government bonds. No doubt the minister is well aware that our bonds are travelling well above par at the present time, and1 it seems to me that financial institutions generally recognize that we are solvent. I think we are just as honourable as any other part of Canada, and I should like to impress that fact upon the minister. It seems to me that, without going into all this litigation the minister is talking about, we could still ask for the benefit of the act.

The difficulty is that we cannot operate the act differently in one province from what we do in the other eight provinces. I know a great deal about the integrity of the citizens of Saskatchewan, because I dealt with them privately for many years. But it simply is the difficulty of administration, where one finds a law' in direct conflict with the provisions of the measure we are now discussing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
A week ago, when the resolution was under discussion, I asked the minister, as reported at page 3710 of Hansard, whether this section could be expanded to provide, for limited-dividend corporations building homes on property they merely lease rather than own outright. The minister replied:
I can hardly imagine a government agency lending money on houses where the control of the land is not permanently in the government.
The statement the minister has just made is generous on his part; but the thing that bothers me is that, a further extension of what this may mean now having come to light, still more may be involved in the wording of the section. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is, it permits what a week ago the minister could not imagine the government doing.

I could not imagine it then, but I find now there is a reason for it. In grants to mining companies or paper mills it is quite often the policy not to sell but to give long-term leases. If a lease is for ninty-nine years, that is regarded as suitable security. May I say that when I spoke a week ago I spoke in good faith, because I understood that the sole purpose of the amendment was to take care of the situation at Banff and Jasper.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not doubt the minister's good faith of a week ago, but I doubt his judgment now.
Perhaps so.

I feel the minister would have every justification to make it possible for

residents to build on crown lands in national parks which they intend to hold in perpetuity. After the word "lessee", he can add two or three words such as "of crown lands", or their legal equivalent, which would make it possible to provide housing on crown lands that are national playgrounds or resorts. I take strong objection to money being lent by the Canadian people to individuals who are simply tenants of large corporations which are exerting a permanent hold on any given property. It seems to me that this provision would not be dangerous if it referred to land in the hands of either the dominion or a provincial government, but beyond that I feel the the minister should not go.
We do not want to perpetuate the land holding system of England which, as the minister knows, is now causing considerable difficulty in connection with the housing programme. Even before the present Labour government came into power, there was trouble because of the manner in which land was held by family corporations. It seems to me that we are moving backward rather than forward if we leave this section unchanged. The minister has said that the purpose of this was simply to make it possible to build in national playgrounds. Why not state it in that way and let the other people sell their land rather than just lease the right to build houses?

I want to refer again to the lending value. If the minister cannot give us the cost per square foot I wonder if he can give us some idea of what percentage of the total cost of a small house, say one costing up to $7,000, the prospective home owner has to put up? In the example I cited to-day, it appears he would have to put up 32 per cent. If the corporation and the lending institution put up only 68 per cent we are not very much better off than we were before we had the act. It is my understanding that private lending institutions will lend 60 per cent as a normal practice.

A four-roomed house built in Vancouver under integrated housing, in which case there is a cost limitation, costing about $5,500 would require an equity of about $600. In the case of a house costing in the neighbourhood of $6,500, the equity would run as high as $1,000. That is under integrated housing where profit limitation applies to the contractor.

I understand that, but am I to assume that it is the policy of the government to presume that, in the cases of houses built by ordinary contractors for veterans and others under part I of the act, exorbitant amounts are allowed for profit? Is that the

Housing Act
basis of distinction between an integrated housing scheme and one carried on under part I?

We have no way of checking the profit made on a house not built under a government plan. If a contractor cares to limit his profits and operate under integrated housing he would have the benefits of priority for materials and so on. We assume that the only reason a contractor would not want to qualify under that scheme is that he wanted more profit than was allowed.

I do not want to get into a theoretical argument and I know the minister does not, but surely some practical figures must be available with relation to loans to home owners under part I of the act within the last six months or so which would give us some idea.

I would say it varies a great deal. Certainly he could get no more favourable terms than those I have quoted if they operated under integrated housing, but they may be much higher if the builder is taking a larger profit.

According to the minister's statement the other day, the present cost of houses is estimated at 150 per cent of the 1939 cost. Why not find out what the cost of a house is to-day and work out your lending value in relation to that rather than use a base line which, so far as I can find out, is not used by any other agency?
I do not know anyone who is building more houses than the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. We know to a gnat's eyebrow how much it costs to-day as compared with the cost in 1939.

I am still not satisfied with paragraph (a). Will the minister explain just why that clause is left wide open for the building of houses on leased property? Is the minister quite happy over the fact that by the terms of this bill any Landlord may ultimately acquire a house which a tenant has put on his property and paid for? That will be the ultimate goal of various individuals who will use this legislation. Why could this paragraph not be reworded?

I am not very keen anyway about the section and I would be quite willing to limit it to parks. However, I am told that that would prevent the building of certain projects in northern Quebec where the transfer of property is not possible, but where it is possible to obtain a ninety-nine year lease. I believe this has something to do with the mining laws of the province.

I would suggest adding the phrase "of crown land" after the word "lessee", or some equivalent wording. Then this concession could be made where the land is perpetually owned by the people of Canada in the right either of the dominion or of a province. If it is held by some corporation which is simply subleasing the mineral rights, then I think we are starting up a dangerous business. I should like the minister to give some assurance on that point.

I do not know about the other provinces, but in my province we have continued the old English practice whereby land is leased for building purposes on longterm leases, 99 years or 999 years. I have drawn up hundreds of such leases. In many cases, the owners of the land do not wish to dispose of the fee simple and they divide up their land into building lots which they refuse to sell. The land upon which my home is built is under such lease. I have not approached the lady who owns the land, but I know others in the vicinity have and she definitely refuses to dispose of the fee simple. These particular leases are for 999 years. There are quite a few in northern New Brunswick and some in the city of Saint John. Whether the practice should be encouraged or not, I am not prepared to say. The fact remains that the practice has become established, some people happen to be in possession of a lot of land under leases of that kind, and unless the act is amended as suggested they would not be eligible to operate under it. Insurance companies, for instance, when they hear of these leases inquire about them and, when they find what the situation is, they withdraw any objection which they otherwise would have to shorter leases. If the leases are confined to longterm leases I do not see anything objectionable about it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Subsection 4B(1) deals with the matter which has just been under discussion. The minister, when speaking on integrated housing, gave a short outline of the plan and statistics as to the number of projects that have been launched and the number of units included. Can he give the committee a little more information about this plan with particular reference to costs, selling prices of homes under it and what has been the experience thus far? Housing Act

Under the agreement the builder agrees: (a) to provide land in any urban area; (b) to erect a specified number of houses thereon; (c) to apply for a loan under the National Housing Act in respect of each house; (d) to offer each house for sale for the approved lending value and certain carrying charges, plus the sum of $350 in the case of a two-room house, $425 in the case of a three-room house, and $500 in the case of a four-room house; and (e) to give preference to veterans in the sale of such houses.

Under section 4B, subsection 3 (b) it is provided:
that such other things shall be done as the corporation deems necessary in order to carry out the intent of this section and to safeguard the interests of His Majesty.
There is, on the face of it, no great objection to that provision, except that it does seem to be very wide, and as such, I think, might be open to objections in the future, when possibly the corporation will say that it will require a prospective owner to cany out this or that undertaking, and the owner may say, "Well, that is not in the act." I think it might be desirable to have defined more specifically what is the intent, and within what range the corporation may make regulations under this subsection. Would the minister take that under consideration?

I shall be very glad to. I think this is a special arrangement to meet a special condition. In other words, at the present time the demand is for houses for veterans, and low-cost housing is required; profit margins must be rigidly controlled. It may be that in later years the demand will be for another type of house, perhaps for others than that for veterans. It may fill up the demand for low-cost housing for veterans and require a different type of house. I think it is simply a flexible provision which will allow the regulations to be amended accordingly.

The only thing I am trying to get at is this: in what sorts of categories may the corporation make these regulations? Will it be for planning, standards of construction, standards of maintenance, times and methods of repayment; or what categories of expression are intended to be given to the corporation under this subsection?

This is an integrated housing plan: it simply provides for financing a contractor to build houses of a certain class with a profit limitation. As I say, present regulations require conditions which apply to the present day; in other words, it covers only low-cost housing for sale to veterans. I am
simply pointing out that under this clause it may be desirable at a later date to encourage contractors to build another type of house, and this is a clause which provides that the regulations may be geared as the times may indicate.	-

speechtext: I am still not satisfied as to the basis for the limited profit which is supposed to accrue to the builder per unit.

priced above the market price. Under the guarantee we are obliged to take it off his hands at the price under the agreement. Yes.

Because some are quite distinct; they are merely dealing with the export of logs. I think it might help 'things if the words "logging and lumbering" were put in that paragraph, because we regard those as two distinct operations.

There is only one other point I should like to make, on the same subject. I am not at all
[Mr. Howe.l
sure that the eighty per cent of the loan is adequate. I have had it represented to me that some of these logging and lumber companies . have already invested practically all their fluid capital in the construction of mills. I can quote one instance where a new mill has been constructed, where new bunkhouses have been put up, and where thirty-five houses have been constructed by that company. The management of that, company have written in to me that they are at the end of their available capital and that the eighty per cent is not adequate to enable them to finance another building project. With reference to this section, I wish to thank the minister very much for having introduced this legislation at the present session. During my travels through the constituency last winter, I found that one of the greatest causes of dissatisfaction among the workers in basic industries was the fact that the National Housing Act was not applicable to them in unorganized communities. I brought back a suggestion to the minister that something might be worked out along the present lines, and I wish to thank the president of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Mr. Mansur, for the excellent work he did in preparing the legislation.
It is about time we realized the great debt we owe the workers in our basic industries who have left their homes and gone to isolated places where they have contributed so much to the economic welfare of the country. During the war period, we lost some of our best loggers. Jobs were available in the cities and in the shipyards where they needed the type of workers we have; loggers are men capable of handling large and heavy loads and heavy equipment, and the men have now found that they do not wish to return to the woods if they cannot take their families with them. I do not blame them. The logger has become tired of endorsing his cheque every month and sending it a distance of two or three hundred miles to his family, simply having enough money once a year to get home for the Christmas holidays.
There has been some criticism of the minister as evidenced by the question that some people ask as to where the jobs are

Housing Act
coming from to employ the owners or the tenants of these homes in the urban areas. It is said that you are building homes in the cities, and it is suggested that the greatest feature about it is that these people will be close to the unemployment insurance office. In my opinion it is important to provide homes for men where there are jobs to be had, and in this legislation provision is 'being made to that end. As the hon. member for Nanaimo has said, it is difficult for companies that are trying to finance their operations, particularly under the present ceiling price of lumber in Canada, to provide extra working capital for the erection of homes for their employees.
One thing I might mention is this. One of the great causes of dissatisfaction in the lumber strike in British Columbia is the fact that a great many men have to travel two hours each way to and from work. Men working in Alberni have to travel two hours out in the morning and two hours back at night, so that they are actually working a twelve-hour day instead of putting in eight hours. Under this provision, the company could provide homes and that would obviate one cause of dissatisfaction.
One thing I would suggest to the minister- and I have discussed- it with him to some extent-is the desirability of bringing fishermen under this section. It is confined to mining and lumbering operations, and I would appreciate it if the minister would give consideration to the fishing industry, bringing it under the same provisions as are extended to the others.
As regards cooperatives, about which we have been speaking, the minister is not partial to providing them with that type of loan. I believe that in my own constituency-and I have no doubt that other coastal members from British Columbia would say the same thing-we have fishing cooperatives of considerable substance, as the minister would discover, and they would probably be eligible for loans under a fishing section of this act. They would be excellent risks, and I can see no reason why they should not come under the heading of incorporated companies. I offer that as a suggestion to the minister.

When I visited the Pacific coast last winter I was greatly impressed with the necessity for the type of housing covered by this section, but I had difficulty in working it out, and the advice of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was helpful to myself and the department in finding a solution which we believe will be workable. I wish to make that acknowledgement at this
time. I have an amendment which will include the fishing industry, and I would ask the Minister of Justice to move:
That subsections 1 and 2 of section 9A of the act, as enacted by clause 15 of the bill, be repealed and the following substituted:
"9A. (1) The corporation may on behalf of His Majesty, and with the approval of the governor in council, make a loan to a borrower engaged in the mining, lumbering, logging or fishing industry, to assist in the construction of low or moderate-cost housing projects in areas or localities that are adjacent to or connected with the operations of the borrower.
(2) For the purpose of this section the expression 'borrower' means an incorporated company engaged in the mining, lumbering, logging or fishing industry, and includes a company (in this section referred to as a 'subsidiary company') incorporated for the purpose of owning, constructing and managing a housing project, all the share capital of which, except directors' qualifying shares, are owned by an incorporated company (in this section referred to as the 'parent company') engaged in the mining, lumbering, logging or fishing industry."
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I so move.
Amendment agreed to.

I hope that does not preclude some questions on the section as amended. Under a concession such as this, will the minister explain why a company which is borrowing from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is favoured with a four per cent rate, while a cooperative, if it can borrow, has to pay 41 per cent? I should like some explanation of that.

May I ask whether, in the opinion of the experts of the department, for the purposes of this section an incorporated company may include a cooperative company, provided that it is definitely associated for the purposes specified in the section?
If the cooperative is also a lumbering or logging company it will qualify.
Or a fishing company?
A cooperative simply for the building of houses in a lumbering area would not.
If it is a cooperative logging company it will be covered?
Yes.
Would it include fishing companies?

Hon. members will remember that there is a 4J per cent rate for home owners and privately owned rental houses. In the case of loans to limited-dividend companies a three per cent rate is available. It is felt that outlying area loans should be at a
Housing Act

rate between three and 4\ per cent. The rate should be lower than per cent, because in every case we have the guarantee of the lumbering or mining company. Further, the company is subject to limitation of earnings on investment to the rate established for the mortgage. Therefore the mortgage rate must have relation to a fair maximum rate allowable on the company's equity. On the other hand, the rate should be higher than three per cent for limited-dividend companies, if for no other reason than that the housing will be of great advantage to lumbering and mining companies. In the light of these factors, we felt that a four per cent rate was appropriate.

I should like to ask the minister the position in connection with lumbering camps, particularly. I realize that mining towns have more stability, more permanence, and it seems to me that lumber camps are fleeting things.
It is just the opposite.

All right; you tell the minister that when I have finished. If a logging operation runs out, what is the position if we have what are called ghost towns? What is the position if the project is abandoned?

The corporation must exercise care to see that the life of the loan is not longer than the life of the community or the operation. In my discussion of the bill this afternoon, I mentioned that the best possible advice must be obtained from appropriate authorities as to the life of the operation, and as to the appropriate type of housing. For example, housing for a short-term operation probably would be built on skids so it could be moved to another operation, if that were appropriate; but skill must be exercised by the corporation to see that their loan is protected, having regard to the nature of the operation.

Under subsection 6, which has to do with the terms of the contract, paragraph (a) reads shortly that the loan can be made only if evidence satisfactory to the corporation has been furnished as to the need for such housing accommodation-a perfectly proper provision-and that such housing accommodation will result in an increased number of people being employed in connection with the operation. It would seem to me that if there were a switch from bunkhouses to houses, so that people working in the operation were able to bring their families there, the purposes of the plan would be served. Surely it would not be necessary that these beautiful houses should bring many mere
[Mr. ITowe.l
people into the employ of the company. It seems to me that a logging operation or a mine has a set crew, and presumably they are there now even without the houses, if the project is being operated properly. I was going to suggest to the minister, in the first place, that this second provision, with regard to an increased number of people being employed, should be dropped altogether, or, in the alternative, that it be amended to provide that an increased number of people should reside in the area of the operation or in connection with the operation, rather than being restricted to an actual addition to the crew employed on the job. I think, too, that the retention of the men employed on one of these operations is perhaps just as important as increasing their number. One thing we should try to guard against is a continual turnover of men because they must go down to the cities to see their friends and their families. The house resumed from Friday, July 26, consideration in committee of bill No. 250, respecting judges of dominion and provincial courts-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 3-Eligibility.

We had not finished the general discussion, I think, Mr. Chairman.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I think we were on section 3 when the committee rose.

It was my recollection that the hon. member for Cariboo had asked a lot of questions which were not answered. I wish to ask the minister about the provision for a division between a judge and his wfife of the retirement allowance allotted to a judge on his retirement. I believe that, under section 26 of the Judges Act, county court and circuit court judges are retired compulsorily when they reach the age of seventy-five years. Under section 26A, w'hich was enacted on August 15, 1944, it was provided that the judges mentioned in sections 23 and 25 might arrange that a portion of their retirement allowance would be payable to their wives. If I have correctly read sections 23 and 25, the option was not extended to county court judges or judges of the circuit court for the district of Montreal. I may tell the minister that I am referring for the moment in particular to county court judges. In fact, was the option not extended to them?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It was, [DOT] in fact, extended to them, but perhaps it would be more convenient for the members if we had this discussion when we get to the pertinent section of the bill, because it is dealt with in 63260-254i
this bill. This bill purports to reproduce what was done in that regard in 1944, and there are sections which expressly deal with it.

I am willing to accept the minister's suggestion, but I thought that if we were still discussing the general terms of the bill, and since there are a number of sections involved, it might be more convenient to do it now. I am going to suggest to the minister-and I am doing it at the instance of the hon. member for Calgary West-that judges of the county courts who, under section 26, were forced to retire when they became seventy-five years old, might now be permitted, by an appropriate amendment, to make the option which was denied to them by section 26A, subsection 1 (a). It does not mean any increase in salary or any more money, but it would ease the minds of those county court judges who were retired before section 26A, subsection 1 (a) was passed if their wives were permitted to avail themselves of the benefits granted by that subsection. It affects a very small number of judges, a group which is rapidly diminishing, and would dispel a great anxiety which has overtaken many of them, especially in view of the decreased value of the dollar.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think I understand the point the hon. member wishes to make. If I do understand him he wishes to know if it would not be possible in this act to give gentlemen who had become pensioners before the provisions were made in 1944, allowing for an optional division of pension rights, the right to make that option at this time. That matter was under consideration both in 1944 and again at this time. The pension provisions enable the governor in council to issue to a judge who has retired letters patent giving him an annuity, and his right to an annuity then is evidenced by and founded upon his letters patent. It is not by virtue of the statute that he is paid the annuity, but because of the letters patent which have been issued to him establishing that annuity in his favour When he gets those letters patent his contractual rights with the crown have come to an end; he has ceased to be a judge, and he has received a document which is full settlement of what the statute enabled the governor in council to grant him. It was felt in 1944 that these gentlemen, having received everything they were entitled to under the Judges Act, could not or should not be dealt with by amendments to the Judges Act. The amendments were made for those to whom the Judges Act still applied, and they were given the right to exercise an option. That right was extended to them for a period of ninety
Judges Act

days, and it was an irrevocable option. They were all notified that they had the right to exercise the option, and practically all of them did exercise it. But when we considered the preparation of a bill to be introduced at this time we did not think we could deal with this aspect, or with another application which has been before the government for at least twenty-five years; that is to say, for an amendment which would provide pensions for widows of judges. There are, I believe, over three hundred widows of former judges, some of whom are in straitened circumstances. It was felt that we could not deal with this class of retired judges still living unless we dealt with the widows of those who had predeceased them, and we felt that we could not do that until such time as we were putting before parliament something more satisfactory than at present exists with respect to old age pensions. That was the reason we felt that we could not single out one class of Canadians and ask parliament to make provision for them (Until there was something being done generally [DOT]with respect to old age pensions.

speechtext:
It is a good argument ^against the whole bill.

But I felt that it would not be proper to ask parliament, when dealing with the present and the future, to deal with pension provisions for those who had in the past served the country in a judicial capacity. I suppose there was not very much they could do but accept the answer, but I have not had anyone say that it was not a reasonable answer to make. I have had to answer the requests that were submitted to me, that more should be done at this time in this bill than it does provide for, and I have had to say that I did not feel that I should come to parliament and ask parliament to do more at this time .than the bill envisages. It is for that reason ,fMr. St. Laurent.1
that we have kept strictly to the situation which deals with the present and the future.

The matter has been considered?
