I had a few words to say on the first section on Friday last. After I had finished the hon. member for Stanstead

Wheat Policy
(Mr. Hackett) took me severely to task. Since what I said at that time related to salaries,
I think my reply to the hon. gentleman will be in order on this section, because it, too, relates to salaries.
I have listened to the hon. member for Stanstead on many occasions in this house and have appreciated and admired the way in which he could marshal his arguments and his facts, and whether we all agreed on the case he made out, it was certainly appreciated by myself. I was not in the house when he spoke on Friday, and I had only an opportunity of reading his speech in Hansard. May I say I have never seen such a conglomeration of inanities in a speech delivered by a gentleman of his legal standing. But what I take exception to mostly is what he said in regard to myself. It has no basis in fact, either as regards my personal character or as regards the philosophy which I accept and expound. At page 3910 of Hansard he said1:
The argument of the hon. member for Vancouver East is an expression of his own political philosophies; eloquently and cogently stated, I admit.
I do not know whether it was eloquently or cogently stated, but I was certainly dealing with facts. He went on to say:
It is a statement of the doctrine of making everybody equally poor, which is a denial of the system which obtains here, namely, private initiative and competition. His is a socialistic system, a class system. Nobody must emerge ahead of anybody else. Everybody must be on a dead level of competence-or incompetence.
Did anyone in this house; did the hon. member for Stanstead ever in this house, hear me urging that we should bring everyone down to a dead level of poverty? As a matter of fact, everything I have said in this house has been said to try to raise everybody up to a high level of living. Surely, when I urge that the government of Canada should not increase the salaries of those who have already a high standard of living until it has done something to improve the standard of living of those who are grovelling in poverty, that is not to say that I wish to bring everyone down to the same dead level of poverty. If the hon. gentleman has not a better argument than that to put forward against my reasoning, it would be far better for him to hold his peace.
There are many things in his speech that are really not fair to the judges of the country. On the following page, 3910, he says:
To-day the judicial office has gone begging for good men.
That is to say, the judges we have to-day are not good men. I never said anything of that kind, because I believe we have good men as judges. He says:
To-day the judicial office has gone begging for good men. Oh, there are multitudes who are willing to serve. I admit that, but the best men are not available and we need the best men.
I maintain that that is a distinct reflection on the character and ability of the men who act as judges in this country to-day, and it was not I who made that statement. The hon. gentleman ended his speech with a most amazing assertion. He said:
I say to the Minister of Justice, give to the judges an increase in salary; give it to them immediately, that they may protect their own virtue even if the government is not as solicitous of it as it should be.
Surely, if it requires a decent standard of living to maintain one's virtue, my attitude is away ahead of the hon. gentleman's. He wishes to maintain the virtue of a mere handful of people. 1 wish to maintain the virtue of the whole of the people of Canada. That is the difference between the doctrine that is held by my hon. friend and the doctrine that is held by myself, and certainly I am not ashamed of my doctrine.
I have served the people of my community for the past twenty-five years. I served them first on the school board in my city; I served them later as alderman in the city council, and 'by virtue of the service I gave at that time I am here. I would1 not !be here if I were advocating such a doctrine as my hon. friend would have the members of the house believe I am advocating. As a matter of fact, his whole speech is all the proof that is required of the bankruptcy of his social thinking.
Section stands.
